name: Acute Coronary Syndrome
description: Spectrum of conditions from unstable angina to NSTEMI and STEMI, caused by acute reduction in coronary blood flow.

epidemiology.incidence: 3 million STEMI, 4 million NSTEMI annually worldwide

pathophysiology: Plaque rupture or erosion with superimposed thrombosis causing partial or complete coronary occlusion.

stemi: Fibrinolysis if PCI not available within 120 min

prognosis: Primary PCI reduces STEMI mortality to <5%

description: Diabetic ketoacidosis (DKA) is a life-threatening complication of diabetes characterized by hyperglycemia, ketosis, and metabolic acidosis. It is most commonly seen in type 1 diabetes but can also occur in type 2 diabetes under certain conditions.

name: Diabetic Ketoacidosis

pathophysiology.mechanism: DKA results from insulin deficiency and counter-regulatory hormone excess, leading to increased hepatic glucose production, impaired glucose utilization, and lipolysis, which in turn leads to ketone production and acidosis.

pathophysiology.progression: If untreated, DKA progresses rapidly to dehydration, electrolyte imbalances, and potentially to coma and death.

prognosis.natural_history: Leads to severe dehydration, electrolyte imbalances, coma, and death if untreated.
prognosis.with_treatment: Good prognosis with prompt treatment; most patients experience full recovery.

description: Myasthenia Gravis is an autoimmune neuromuscular disorder characterized by weakness and rapid fatigue of voluntary muscles. It results from an immune-mediated interference in the acetylcholine neurotransmission at the neuromuscular junction.

diagnostic_criteria.gold_standard: Edrophonium test (Tensilon test) or response to acetylcholinesterase inhibitors.

epidemiology.sex_ratio: 1:2 (M:F) under 40, more balanced in older age

name: Myasthenia Gravis

pathophysiology.mechanism: Immune-mediated attack on acetylcholine receptors at the neuromuscular junction.
pathophysiology.molecular_basis: Anti-AChR antibodies in most cases; anti-MuSK antibodies in seronegative MG.
pathophysiology.progression: Variable course with periods of exacerbation and remission; may progress to life-threatening respiratory crisis.

warning_signs: Sudden respiratory distress requiring immediate medical attention

secondary: Regular monitoring for early detection of exacerbations

prognosis.natural_history: Chronic relapsing-remitting condition with potential progression to generalized weakness.

prognosis.recurrence_rate: Low in immunocompetent individuals, higher with anatomical defects

description: Acute pyelonephritis is a sudden and severe kidney infection that causes the kidneys to swell and may lead to permanent damage. It is a serious type of urinary tract infection that usually begins in the lower urinary tract and ascends to the upper urinary tract.

warning_signs: Severe back pain or blood in urine requiring immediate attention

prognosis.natural_history: Can progress to renal scarring and chronic kidney disease if untreated.

special_populations.elderly: Adjust doses of renally cleared drugs

description: Nephrolithiasis refers to the formation of calculi within the kidney, leading to potential obstruction of urine flow and renal colic. It is associated with significant pain and potential complications if left untreated.

pathophysiology.molecular_basis: Genetic predispositions affect calcium, oxalate, and urate metabolism.
pathophysiology.progression: Stones may remain asymptomatic or cause obstruction, pain, infection, or renal damage.

prognosis.natural_history: Spontaneous passage of stones is common for stones <5mm

prognosis.natural_history: Progressive decline over approximately 8-10 years

synonyms: Senile Dementia of the Alzheimer Type

progression.name: Stage I / Early
progression.description: Subclinical or mild cognitive impairment with subtle changes in cognitive function.
progression.criteria: Subjective memory complaints, objective memory impairment on testing.
progression.management: Lifestyle changes, cognitive stimulation therapies, regular monitoring.

progression.name: Stage II / Mild-Moderate
progression.description: Noticeable memory and cognitive changes affecting daily life.
progression.criteria: Difficulty in performing complex tasks; noticeable memory loss.
progression.management: Cholinesterase inhibitors such as donepezil, supportive therapies.

progression.name: Stage III / Moderate-Severe
progression.description: Marked deficits in cognitive and functional abilities.
progression.criteria: Assistance required with daily activities, significant memory deficits.
progression.management: Addition of NMDA receptor antagonist memantine, increased caregiving.

progression.name: Stage IV / End-stage
progression.description: Profound cognitive and functional impairments, total assistance needed.
progression.criteria: Severe memory loss and impairment in communication, fully dependent.
progression.management: Palliative care focus, advanced caregiving, safety measures.

description: Atherosclerotic heart disease, commonly known as coronary artery disease, involves the narrowing or blockage of coronary arteries due to the accumulation of atherosclerotic plaques.

diagnostic_criteria.criteria_name: Not specific to atherosclerotic heart disease
diagnostic_criteria.interpretation: Diagnosis is made based on clinical history, ECG changes, and imaging studies.

history: Assess history of smoking, diet, physical activity, and family history of heart disease.
imaging: Chest X-ray for cardiac size and pulmonary vasculature
CT angiogram for coronary arteries
special_tests: Electrocardiogram (ECG)
Exercise stress test
Echocardiography

epidemiology.prevalence: Approximately 6% of adults over 20 years in the U.S. have been diagnosed with coronary artery disease.
epidemiology.incidence: Around 1.5 million new cases are diagnosed annually in the United States.
epidemiology.demographics: More prevalent in men over 45 and women over 55, with higher incidence in Caucasians and African Americans compared to other ethnic groups.

causes: Accumulation of cholesterol and fatty deposits on the arterial walls.
risk_factors: Modifiable: smoking, hypertension, high cholesterol, obesity, physical inactivity, diet
Non-modifiable: age, family history, male gender
etiology.pathophysiology: Atherosclerosis involves the deposition of lipids, calcification, and cellular components in arterial walls, leading to plaque formation which narrows and hardens the arteries, potentially reducing blood flow to the heart muscle.

monitoring.frequency: Every 6-12 months or as needed based on risk assessment
targets: LDL cholesterol < 100 mg/dL in high-risk individuals

name: Atherosclerotic heart disease
patient_education: Significance of lifestyle changes in managing risk
Recognizing symptoms that require immediate medical attention

primary: Regular screening for hypertension and cholesterol
prevention.screening: Lipid profile screening every 4-6 years for adults aged 20 and older.

prognosis.natural_history: Gradual progression can lead to myocardial infarction, heart failure, or arrhythmias if untreated.
prognosis.with_treatment: Optimal treatment improves survival and quality of life, reducing the risk of heart attacks.

non_pharmacological: Dietary modifications to reduce saturated fats and cholesterol

pharmacological.indication: To reduce heart rate and blood pressure

ldl_cholesterol.evidence: Impaired LDL uptake leads to elevated serum LDL levels.

description: Heart failure is a clinical syndrome characterized by the heart's inability to pump sufficient blood to meet the body's needs. The unspecified category does not differentiate between left-sided or right-sided failure.

criteria: Major: Paroxysmal nocturnal dyspnea, neck vein distension, pulmonary rales
Minor: Ankle edema, nocturnal cough, dyspnea on exertion
diagnostic_criteria.interpretation: Diagnosis requires the presence of either 2 major criteria or 1 major and 2 minor criteria.

history: History of heart disease or hypertension
imaging: Chest X-ray
Echocardiogram
special_tests: Electrocardiogram (ECG)

epidemiology.incidence: About 650,000 new cases are diagnosed annually in the United States.

risk_factors: Modifiable: smoking, obesity, sedentary lifestyle, high dietary salt intake
Non-modifiable: age, gender, family history, congenital heart defects
etiology.pathophysiology: Heart failure results from damage to the myocardium, leading to either systolic dysfunction (impaired contraction) or diastolic dysfunction (impaired filling). This results in reduced cardiac output and compensatory mechanisms such as neurohormonal activation.

monitoring.frequency: Regular follow-up every 3-6 months or sooner if symptoms worsen.

name: Heart failure, unspecified

prevention.screening: Focus on high-risk populations with echocardiograms and regular check-ups.

description: Atrial fibrillation (AF) is a common supraventricular arrhythmia characterized by disorganized atrial electrical activity and ineffective atrial contraction.

description: Acute myocardial infarction (AMI) is a condition characterized by the interruption of blood supply to a part of the heart, causing heart cells to die. 'Unspecified' refers to cases without further specification of location.

diagnostic_criteria.criteria_name: Fourth Universal Definition of Myocardial Infarction
criteria: Detection of a rise and/or fall of cardiac biomarker values (preferably cardiac troponin) with at least one value above the 99th percentile upper reference limit and at least one of the following: symptoms of ischemia, new or presumed new significant ST-T wave changes or new left bundle branch block, development of pathological Q waves, imaging evidence of new loss of viable myocardium, or identification of a coronary thrombus by angiography or autopsy
diagnostic_criteria.interpretation: Criteria met establishes diagnosis; requires correlation with clinical findings.

Risk factors for coronary artery disease
imaging: Chest X-ray to rule out other causes of chest pain
special_tests: Electrocardiogram (ECG)

epidemiology.incidence: Globally, millions of people experience an acute myocardial infarction yearly, with significant variation by region.
epidemiology.demographics: Most commonly affects middle-aged to older adults, more prevalent in males, though risk equalizes with increasing age among genders.

etiology.pathophysiology: The pathophysiology involves the rupture of an atherosclerotic plaque and subsequent thrombosis, leading to myocardial ischemia and necrosis.

monitoring.frequency: Continuous monitoring during acute phase, daily or as needed later

description: Angina pectoris is characterized by chest pain or discomfort due to inadequate blood flow to the heart muscle (myocardial ischemia), often provoked by exertion or emotional stress.

diagnostic_criteria.interpretation: Diagnosis is clinical, supported by ECG changes and response to nitroglycerin; exclusion of other causes of chest pain is important.

history: Characteristics of chest pain (onset, location, duration, intensity), associated symptoms, risk factor assessment, exercise tolerance
physical_exam: Cardiovascular exam to check for murmurs, peripheral pulses, and bruits
imaging: Chest X-ray to rule out other causes of chest pain
special_tests: Resting ECG, Stress testing (exercise ECG or myocardial perfusion imaging), Coronary angiography for high-risk patients

epidemiology.demographics: Angina is more common in men over 45 and women over 55, with higher rates in people of South Asian or African descent.

etiology.pathophysiology: The primary mechanism is an imbalance between myocardial oxygen supply and demand, typically due to coronary artery obstruction from atherosclerotic plaque.

monitoring.frequency: Every 3 to 6 months
targets: LDL cholesterol < 70 mg/dL in high-risk patients

ros_level.evidence: Increased ROS levels can lead to oxidative stress, damaging lung tissue and contributing to failure.

apoptotic_index.evidence: Increased apoptosis in lung cells can be a response to severe respiratory damage, exacerbating failure.

description: Non-ST Elevation Myocardial Infarction (NSTEMI) is a type of heart attack characterized by the absence of persistent ST-segment elevation on ECG, involving partial occlusion of a coronary artery and leading to myocardial necrosis.

pathophysiology.progression: Progresses to complete myocardial necrosis if untreated, can lead to heart failure.

name: Hypertrophic Cardiomyopathy
description: Hypertrophic cardiomyopathy (HCM) is a genetic disease characterized by disproportionate ventricular hypertrophy, often asymmetrical, predominantly affecting the septum. It can lead to functional impairment and is a common cause of sudden cardiac death in young athletes.

epidemiology.mortality: 1-2% annual risk of sudden cardiac death
epidemiology.age_distribution: Peak incidence in adolescence and early adulthood
epidemiology.geographic_variation: Worldwide distribution with no specific high-prevalence regions

pathophysiology.mechanism: HCM is characterized by thickened heart muscle, particularly the interventricular septum, which can obstruct blood flow and affect heart function.
pathophysiology.molecular_basis: Mutations in genes encoding sarcomere proteins
pathophysiology.progression: Progressive hypertrophy can lead to heart failure, arrhythmias, and sudden cardiac death.

signs.interpretation: Suggestive of left ventricular outflow obstruction

diagnostic_criteria.gold_standard: Echocardiography showing septal hypertrophy of 15 mm or more in the absence of other causes

laboratory_findings.timing: At diagnosis or if family history is present

additional.advantages: Higher resolution and better tissue characterization

differential_diagnosis.key_differentiator: Presence of gallop rhythm on auscultation

special_populations.elderly: Dose adjustments due to renal function

prognosis.natural_history: Progression to heart failure and risk of sudden cardiac death
prognosis.with_treatment: Reduced symptoms and decreased risk of sudden death

warning_signs: New onset of syncope or palpitations

s3_present.evidence: Heart failure or diastolic dysfunction can manifest as an S3 gallop in hypertrophic cardiomyopathy.

jvp.evidence: Jugular venous pressure may be elevated due to impaired ventricular filling and increased venous return pressure.

echo_ef.evidence: Ejection fraction may be normal or hyperdynamic in hypertrophy due to increased contractility.

name: Restrictive Cardiomyopathy
description: Restrictive cardiomyopathy is characterized by impaired ventricular filling due to decreased ventricular compliance with typically normal systolic function. It results in diastolic heart failure and is often secondary to other infiltrative diseases.

epidemiology.age_distribution: Affects all age groups but more common in older adults
epidemiology.geographic_variation: Higher prevalence in regions with higher incidence of diseases like amyloidosis and sarcoidosis

pathophysiology.mechanism: The disease involves stiffening of myocardial tissue leading to poor ventricular filling. Infiltrative conditions often cause rigidity, reducing compliance.
pathophysiology.molecular_basis: Genetic mutations in sarcomeric proteins or storage diseases
pathophysiology.progression: Progresses from mild diastolic dysfunction to severe heart failure

name: Ventricular Fibrillation
description: Ventricular fibrillation (VF) is a life-threatening cardiac arrhythmia characterized by uncoordinated contractions of the ventricles, resulting in the cessation of effective blood circulation.

pathophysiology.mechanism: Caused by chaotic electrical activity in the ventricles leading to loss of coordinated contraction and cardiac output.
pathophysiology.molecular_basis: Associated with ion channel mutations affecting cardiac repolarization.
pathophysiology.progression: Can be preceded by ventricular tachycardia and rapidly leads to cardiac arrest.

name: Sick Sinus Syndrome
description: Sick Sinus Syndrome is a collection of heart rhythm disorders due to malfunction of the sinus node, manifesting as tachycardia, bradycardia, or sinus arrest. It often results in fatigability, dizziness, or syncope.

epidemiology.incidence: 3 cases per 10,000 person-years in older adults
epidemiology.mortality: Elevated mortality related to bradyarrhythmias and heart failure

pathophysiology.mechanism: Malfunction or degeneration of the sinus node leads to impaired impulse generation.
pathophysiology.molecular_basis: Associated with fibrotic degeneration of nodal tissue
pathophysiology.progression: Can progress to symptomatic arrhythmias and heart failure if untreated

name: Aortic Regurgitation
description: Aortic regurgitation is a condition characterized by the backflow of blood from the aorta into the left ventricle due to inadequate closure of the aortic valve. It can lead to volume overload of the left ventricle and subsequent heart failure if untreated.

epidemiology.geographic_variation: Higher prevalence in rheumatic heart disease regions

pathophysiology.mechanism: Primary mechanism involves retrograde blood flow from the aorta to the left ventricle due to valve incompetence, leading to left ventricular volume overload and dilation.
pathophysiology.molecular_basis: Associated with genetic mutations affecting connective tissue, such as in Marfan syndrome.
pathophysiology.progression: Untreated, it can progress to chronic heart failure due to left ventricular dilatation and hypertrophy.

name: Mitral Stenosis
description: Mitral stenosis is characterized by narrowing of the mitral valve opening, impeding blood flow from the left atrium to the left ventricle, often resulting from chronic rheumatic heart disease.

epidemiology.mortality: 20% 5-year mortality after symptom onset without treatment

pathophysiology.mechanism: Leaflet thickening and commissural fusion due to chronic inflammatory process, leading to valve stenosis.
pathophysiology.molecular_basis: Rheumatic inflammation post-streptococcal infection causing valvular fibrosis.
pathophysiology.progression: Progressive narrowing leading to chronic increased left atrial pressure and pulmonary hypertension.

name: Mitral Valve Prolapse
description: Mitral Valve Prolapse (MVP) is a valvular heart disorder where the mitral valve does not close properly, causing it to bulge or prolapse into the left atrium during systole. This can lead to mitral regurgitation and other complications.

epidemiology.mortality: Low, unless complications such as severe mitral regurgitation occur

pathophysiology.mechanism: The mitral valve leaflets and chordae tendineae become myxomatous and redundant, leading to improper closure.
pathophysiology.molecular_basis: Often associated with mutations in collagen genes, such as COL1A1 and COL1A2.
pathophysiology.progression: Can progress to significant mitral regurgitation and atrial fibrillation if left untreated.

epidemiology.geographic_variation: Higher in South America due to schistosomiasis

pathophysiology.mechanism: Increased pulmonary vascular resistance leads to increased workload on the right side of the heart, eventually causing right heart failure.
pathophysiology.molecular_basis: BMPR2 gene mutations are implicated in idiopathic cases.
pathophysiology.progression: Gradual increase in pulmonary arterial pressure causes progressive heart failure.

name: Chronic Cough

pathophysiology.mechanism: Chronic cough may result from persistent irritation, inflammation, or increased sensitivity of cough receptors in the airways.
pathophysiology.molecular_basis: Involves complex neurogenic inflammatory pathways and heightened sensitivity of capsaicin-sensitive C-fibers.
pathophysiology.progression: Chronic cough can lead to complications such as chronic irritation of the throat, sleep disturbances, and life quality impairment.

name: Helicobacter pylori Infection
description: Helicobacter pylori infection is a common condition caused by a Gram-negative bacterium that colonizes the gastric epithelium, leading to gastritis, peptic ulcer disease, and increased risk of gastric cancer.

epidemiology.incidence: Variable based on region and population dynamics
epidemiology.mortality: Around 1% in cases of associated gastric cancer
epidemiology.age_distribution: Common in adults over 40, but can affect all ages

pathophysiology.mechanism: H. pylori damages the protective mucous lining of the stomach, leading to inflammation, ulceration, and potential malignancy.
pathophysiology.molecular_basis: Virulence factors include CagA and VacA peptides which disrupt epithelial cell integrity and immune response.
pathophysiology.progression: Persistent infection can lead to chronic gastritis, peptic ulcer disease, mucosa-associated lymphoid tissue (MALT) lymphoma, and gastric cancer.

pathophysiology.molecular_basis: Potential involvement of nitric oxide synthase pathways and interstitial cells of Cajal abnormalities.
pathophysiology.progression: Chronic progression with episodes of acute flares, often affecting quality of life.

name: Intracerebral Hemorrhagic Stroke
description: An intracerebral hemorrhagic stroke is a type of stroke where bleeding occurs within the brain tissue itself, leading to neurological deterioration and high mortality if untreated.

epidemiology.age_distribution: Most commonly affects older adults, particularly those over 60
epidemiology.geographic_variation: Higher incidence in Asia and sub-Saharan Africa

pathophysiology.mechanism: Rupture of small penetrating arteries within the brain parenchyma leading to bleeding.
pathophysiology.molecular_basis: Arterial wall damage due to chronic hypertension or amyloid deposition.
pathophysiology.progression: Rapid onset with potential for expansion and mass effect leading to herniation.

symptoms.name: sudden onset headache

laboratory_findings.interpretation: Rule out other causes like infection

additional.indication: Assessment of hematoma age, underlying lesions
findings: gradient echo sequences show blooming artifact

distinguishing_features: CT showing ischemia rather than bleed
CT shows blood in subarachnoid space

special_populations.renal_impairment: Dose adjustments of medications as needed

prognosis.natural_history: High risk of rapid deterioration and potentially fatal without treatment.
prognosis.with_treatment: Improved outcomes with rapid, appropriate intervention.

name: Lewy Body Dementia
description: Lewy Body Dementia is a progressive neurodegenerative disorder characterized by dementia with notable fluctuations in cognition and recurrent visual hallucinations, and Parkinsonism.

pathophysiology.mechanism: Accumulation of alpha-synuclein protein forming Lewy bodies in brain regions.
pathophysiology.molecular_basis: Genetic factors may play a role, with mutations in GBA and SNCA possibly implicated.
pathophysiology.progression: Progressive cognitive decline with worsening motor and autonomic symptoms over several years.

pathophysiology.progression: Progressive decline in behavioral and executive functions eventually leading to severe cognitive impairment.

name: Trigeminal Neuralgia
description: Trigeminal Neuralgia is a chronic pain condition affecting the trigeminal nerve, which carries sensation from the face to the brain. It is characterized by episodes of intense, stabbing, electric-shock-like pain typically on one side of the face.

epidemiology.mortality: 0% directly but affects quality of life
epidemiology.age_distribution: Most common in individuals over 50 years
epidemiology.geographic_variation: Higher prevalence in Europe and North America

pathophysiology.mechanism: Compression of the trigeminal nerve root by an aberrant loop of artery or vein, leading to demyelination and hyperactivity.
pathophysiology.molecular_basis: Not primarily genetic; demyelination linked to secondary causes such as multiple sclerosis.
pathophysiology.progression: Typically starts with mild symptoms and progresses over weeks to months before stabilizing.

symptoms.name: Facial pain
symptoms.description: Recurrent episodes of severe, unilateral facial pain in the distribution of the trigeminal nerve branches.

signs.technique: Gentle palpation of the facial region

name: Graves' Disease
description: Graves' disease is an autoimmune disorder that leads to hyperthyroidism, or overactive thyroid, characterized by excess thyroid hormone production. It is the most common cause of hyperthyroidism and often presents with eye involvement known as Graves' ophthalmopathy.

epidemiology.mortality: Low with treatment; untreated can lead to serious complications

pathophysiology.mechanism: The disease involves the production of thyroid-stimulating immunoglobulins that mimic TSH, leading to gland hyperactivity.
pathophysiology.molecular_basis: Association with HLA-DR3, and genetic predisposition.
pathophysiology.progression: Chronic with potential for periods of remission and exacerbation.

symptoms.name: Weight loss
symptoms.description: Rapid weight loss despite normal or increased appetite

symptoms.name: Palpitations
symptoms.description: Increased heart rate and sensation of the heart racing

signs.name: Exophthalmos

clinical_presentation.typical_presentation: A young adult with weight loss, heat intolerance, and palpitations, often with a noticeable goiter.

second_line.monitoring: Liver function tests, complete blood count

prognosis.with_treatment: Good, majority achieve euthyroidism

prognosis.mortality: Less than 1% at 5 years with proper management.

monitoring.frequency: Every 6-12 weeks initially, then every 3-6 months once stable

name: Thyroid Nodules and Cancer
description: Thyroid nodules are growths within the thyroid gland, and while most are benign, a small percentage may be malignant. Thyroid cancer is classified into several types, including papillary, follicular, medullary, and anaplastic, based on histopathology.

epidemiology.prevalence: 5% of individuals over 60 have detectable thyroid nodules

pathophysiology.mechanism: Genetic mutations lead to uncontrolled growth of thyroid cells.
pathophysiology.molecular_basis: Mutations in RET, BRAF, and RAS genes commonly found.
pathophysiology.progression: Progression from a nodule to localized cancer, and potential metastasis.

name: Primary Hyperaldosteronism
description: Primary hyperaldosteronism, also known as Conn's syndrome, is an endocrine disorder characterized by excessive production of aldosterone, leading to hypertension and hypokalemia.

epidemiology.mortality: Low directly; indirect through cardiovascular events

pathophysiology.mechanism: Increased aldosterone production by adenoma or hyperplasia leads to sodium retention, potassium excretion, and volume expansion.
pathophysiology.molecular_basis: Mutations in KCNJ5 and other genes
pathophysiology.progression: Chronic hypertension and potential cardiovascular damage if untreated

symptoms.name: Hypertension
symptoms.description: Elevated blood pressure often resistant to conventional therapy

prognosis.with_treatment: Improved BP control and reduced cardiovascular events

secondary: Screening for those with resistant hypertension

potassium.evidence: Aldosterone promotes potassium excretion, leading to hypokalemia.

prognosis.mortality: 5% at 10 years due to cardiovascular complications

monitoring.frequency: monthly monitoring initially, then every 3-6 months once stable

name: Hypoparathyroidism
description: Hypoparathyroidism is a condition characterized by insufficient production of parathyroid hormone (PTH), leading to low calcium levels in the blood, increased phosphorus levels, and resulting muscle cramps and spasms.

pathophysiology.mechanism: Reduced or absent production of parathyroid hormone leads to decreased renal activation of vitamin D and reduced intestinal calcium absorption.
pathophysiology.molecular_basis: Mutations in CASR, PTH, or GCM2 genes can lead to congenital forms.
pathophysiology.progression: Chronic hypocalcemia can result in musculoskeletal, neurological, and cardiovascular complications.

prognosis.with_treatment: Good outcomes with controlled calcium levels

name: Hypopituitarism
description: Hypopituitarism is a clinical syndrome resulting from decreased secretion of one or more pituitary hormones. It is often due to pituitary or hypothalamic disease.

epidemiology.age_distribution: Most commonly diagnosed in middle-aged adults

pathophysiology.mechanism: Destruction or dysfunction of the pituitary gland or hypothalamus leading to hormone deficiencies.
pathophysiology.molecular_basis: Mutations involving POU1F1, PROP1, LHX4 genes may be involved.
pathophysiology.progression: Can progress to total hormone deficiency if untreated.

symptoms.name: Fatigue
symptoms.description: Persistent tiredness not relieved by rest

signs.name: Pallor

clinical_presentation.typical_presentation: Fatigue, weight loss, low blood pressure, and amenorrhea in women.

diagnostic_criteria.gold_standard: Hormonal assays demonstrating deficiencies coupled with MRI findings

name: Granulomatosis with Polyangiitis
description: Granulomatosis with polyangiitis (GPA) is a rare systemic necrotizing vasculitis characterized by granulomatous inflammation predominately affecting the respiratory tract and kidneys.

pathophysiology.mechanism: Autoimmune reaction leading to small-to-medium vessel vasculitis with granuloma formation.
pathophysiology.molecular_basis: Presence of anti-neutrophil cytoplasmic antibodies (ANCAs), particularly PR3-ANCA.
pathophysiology.progression: Without treatment, progresses to renal failure and respiratory compromise.

diagnostic_criteria.gold_standard: Tissue biopsy showing granulomatous inflammation and vasculitis.

differential_diagnosis.key_differentiator: Granulomas absent on biopsy in MPA.

special_populations.hepatic_impairment: Use caution with hepatically cleared drugs

prognosis.natural_history: Untreated GPA may lead to end-stage renal disease and severe respiratory compromise.
prognosis.with_treatment: Most patients achieve remission with treatment.

name: Osteomyelitis
description: Osteomyelitis is an infection of the bone that can be acute or chronic and is most commonly caused by bacteria. It can result in bone destruction and systemic illness if untreated.

epidemiology.geographic_variation: Higher in low-income regions with poor healthcare access

pathophysiology.mechanism: Infection of the bone through hematogenous spread, direct inoculation, or contiguous spread from nearby tissues.
pathophysiology.molecular_basis: Involves biofilm formation by bacteria such as Staphylococcus aureus.
pathophysiology.progression: Initial infection leads to inflammation, bone necrosis, and potential chronic infection with sequestra formation.

symptoms.name: Pain

symptoms.name: Fever

signs.name: Localized tenderness

name: Tetanus
description: Tetanus is a serious bacterial infection caused by Clostridium tetani, characterized by muscle spasms, stiffness, and lockjaw. It requires prompt medical treatment and preventive vaccination strategies.

It often results in persistent concern about additional attacks or significant maladaptive change in behavior related to the attacks.

name: Cardiac Arrest
description: Cardiac arrest is the sudden cessation of cardiac function, resulting in loss of effective circulation. It is a medical emergency requiring immediate intervention to restore circulation and prevent irreversible damage.

epidemiology.mortality: Approximately 90% case fatality when occurring outside a hospital
epidemiology.age_distribution: More common in older adults, peak incidence in people >60 years
