name: Hemophilia B
description: Hemophilia B is a genetic bleeding disorder caused by a deficiency of coagulation factor IX, leading to prolonged bleeding episodes.

epidemiology.geographic_variation: Worldwide distribution with higher prevalence in the UK

pathophysiology.mechanism: Hemophilia B results from mutations in the F9 gene leading to a decrease or absence of factor IX, disrupting the coagulation cascade.
pathophysiology.molecular_basis: Mutations in the F9 gene on the X chromosome
pathophysiology.progression: Chronic disorder with bleeding episodes that can worsen with age if untreated

symptoms.name: Spontaneous bleeding
symptoms.description: Bleeding episodes without trauma, often in joints or muscles.

signs.name: Hemarthrosis
signs.description: Swollen joints with pain due to bleeding.
signs.technique: Joint examination for swelling and tenderness

clinical_presentation.typical_presentation: Recurrent joint bleeds in a young male child with family history of clotting disorders.
atypical_presentations: Intracranial hemorrhage in absence of trauma
red_flags: sudden severe headache indicating possible intracranial bleed

diagnostic_criteria.gold_standard: Quantitative measurement of factor IX activity levels

laboratory_findings.interpretation: Prolonged in patients with factor IX deficiency

differential_diagnosis.key_differentiator: Factor VIII level normal in Hemophilia B

special_populations.pregnancy: Increased monitoring and factor IX levels during delivery

prognosis.natural_history: Chronic joint damage and potential disability without treatment
prognosis.with_treatment: Improved life expectancy and quality of life with prophylaxis

unfavorable: Delayed treatment leading to joint damage

qtc_interval.evidence: Repolarization change due to electrolyte disturbance

lvef.evidence: Due to decreased preload from blood loss

genetic_risk.evidence: X-linked genetic trait for Hemophilia B

name: Sensorineural Hearing Loss
description: Sensorineural hearing loss (SNHL) is a type of hearing loss resulting from damage to the inner ear (cochlea) or the nerve pathways from the inner ear to the brain. It is the most common type of permanent hearing loss.

pathophysiology.mechanism: Damage to the hair cells in the cochlea or atrophy of the auditory nerve fibers leads to impaired sound perception.
pathophysiology.molecular_basis: Genetic mutations (e.g., GJB2) may play a role.
pathophysiology.progression: Often progressive, especially with aging or continued exposure to risk factors.

symptoms.name: Hearing loss
symptoms.description: Gradual reduction in hearing ability, particularly for high-pitched sounds.

signs.name: Positive Rinne's test
signs.description: Air conduction is better than bone conduction.
signs.technique: Perform Rinne's test using a tuning fork

clinical_presentation.typical_presentation: Patient presents with gradual hearing loss, difficulty understanding speech in noisy environments.

diagnostic_criteria.gold_standard: Audiometry

clinical_criteria.name: None specific
clinical_criteria.diagnosis_requires: Audiogram showing hearing loss with no conductive component

classification.criteria: Mild to moderate hearing loss on audiometry

laboratory_findings.interpretation: Determines degree and type of hearing loss

prognosis.natural_history: Progressive hearing decline without treatment
prognosis.with_treatment: Improved hearing with amplification devices

warning_signs: Sudden hearing loss requires urgent evaluation

spo2.evidence: Sensorineural hearing loss does not directly affect respiratory physiology.

respiratory_rate.evidence: No impact on respiratory rate associated with sensorineural hearing loss.

fev1.evidence: No known effects of sensorineural hearing loss on spirometry measurements.

mitochondrial_dysfunction_markers.evidence: Mitochondrial dysfunction is implicated in cases of sensorineural hearing loss, especially in genetic syndromes.

relevant_genes.description: Gene expression changes related to auditory pathway and cochlear function

cochlear_hair_cell_damage.evidence: Damage to cochlear hair cells is a primary pathophysiological change in sensorineural hearing loss.

cognitive_assessment.evidence: Cognitive load effect from hearing loss

cortisol.evidence: Stress response due to hearing loss

homocysteine.evidence: Metabolic component linked to hearing loss

vestibular_function.evidence: Impaired balance mechanisms due to hearing loss

name: Tinnitus
description: Tinnitus is the perception of sound within the human ear in the absence of corresponding external sound. It is often perceived as a ringing or buzzing noise and can severely affect quality of life.

epidemiology.mortality: 0% as it is not a direct cause of mortality

pathophysiology.mechanism: Disruption in the auditory pathways often due to hearing loss, where compensatory neural activity causes perception of sound.
pathophysiology.molecular_basis: Potential involvement of neurotransmitters like glutamate and GABA.
pathophysiology.progression: May remain stable or worsen over time depending on exposure and management.

signs.name: absence of external sound
signs.description: sound only perceived by the patient
signs.technique: patient report in a quiet room

clinical_presentation.typical_presentation: Patient reports a persistent or intermittent sound in one or both ears, often described as ringing.

diagnostic_criteria.gold_standard: Audiological evaluation and patient-reported symptoms

prognosis.natural_history: Can persist or worsen without treatment
prognosis.with_treatment: Variable, some patients experience relief
prognosis.recurrence_rate: Varies as sound perception may fluctuate

secondary: regular hearing tests if at risk

key_points: Tinnitus is common and often linked to hearing loss.
warning_signs: sudden hearing changes require immediate evaluation

muscle_tension.evidence: Neck and shoulder tension due to tinnitus

name: Idiopathic Thrombocytopenic Purpura
description: Idiopathic Thrombocytopenic Purpura (ITP) is an autoimmune disorder characterized by isolated thrombocytopenia without a known cause. It results in an increased risk of bleeding due to anti-platelet antibodies leading to platelet destruction.

epidemiology.age_distribution: Bimodal peak in children <10 and adults >60

pathophysiology.mechanism: Autoantibody-mediated platelet destruction in the spleen and other reticuloendothelial tissues.
pathophysiology.molecular_basis: Involves IgG autoantibodies against platelet glycoproteins such as GPIIb/IIIa.
pathophysiology.progression: Can progress from asymptomatic to chronic with significant bleeding risk.

symptoms.name: Petechiae and Ecchymoses
symptoms.description: Spontaneous bruising and small red spots on the skin.

signs.name: Hematomas
signs.description: Large bruises forming on the body.

clinical_presentation.typical_presentation: Sudden onset of petechiae and ecchymoses in a previously healthy individual.
red_flags: Severe headache indicating possible intracranial bleeding

diagnostic_criteria.gold_standard: Diagnosis of exclusion with isolated thrombocytopenia and no known cause (typically <100,000/μL)

laboratory_findings.expected_value: Reduced platelet count, often large platelets
laboratory_findings.interpretation: Rule out other causes such as pseudothrombocytopenia

differential_diagnosis.key_differentiator: Microangiopathic hemolytic anemia and ADAMTS13 deficiency

special_populations.elderly: Avoid long-term steroids due to side effects
special_populations.hepatic_impairment: Caution with medications metabolized in liver

prognosis.natural_history: Chronic course with spontaneous remissions and relapses
prognosis.with_treatment: Good response in majority, but relapses possible

primary: Avoidance of certain medications known to affect platelets

key_points: Notify doctor if experiencing unusual bleeding

name: Acoustic Neuroma
description: Acoustic neuroma, also known as vestibular schwannoma, is a benign tumor arising from the Schwann cells of the vestibular nerve. It is characterized by its location at the cerebellopontine angle and can cause hearing loss, tinnitus, and balance disturbances.

pathophysiology.mechanism: Proliferation of Schwann cells on vestibular nerve due to genetic mutations.
pathophysiology.molecular_basis: Mutations in the NF2 gene encoding Merlin.
pathophysiology.progression: Slow-growing, may cause compression of cranial nerves and brainstem.

symptoms.name: Unilateral Hearing Loss
symptoms.description: Gradual sensorineural hearing loss in one ear.

signs.name: Positive Rinne Test
signs.description: Air conduction is better than bone conduction in the affected ear.
signs.technique: Tuning fork placed on mastoid then near ear canal.

clinical_presentation.typical_presentation: Gradual onset of unilateral hearing loss and tinnitus, with possible imbalance.
red_flags: Rapidly progressive symptoms suggesting malignant transformation

diagnostic_criteria.gold_standard: MRI with gadolinium contrast showing tumor at cerebellopontine angle

classification.criteria: Tumor confined to internal auditory canal

findings: Bone erosion at internal auditory canal
additional.limitations: Less sensitive than MRI for soft tissues

special_populations.elderly: Consider conservative management due to slower growth

prognosis.natural_history: Progressive hearing loss, possible brainstem compression
prognosis.with_treatment: Good control with surgical and radiosurgical interventions

warning_signs: Worsening hearing loss requiring immediate evaluation

cranial_nerves.finding: Hearing loss in affected ear, facial numbness or weakness

sensory_exam.finding: Intact to light touch except facial numbness

mri.finding: Well-defined mass in the cerebellopontine angle, consistent with acoustic neuroma

ct_scan.finding: Enhancing lesion noted affecting auditory canal

hearing_loss.finding: Sensorineural hearing loss in affected ear

vestibular_test.finding: Positive Dix-Hallpike maneuver in affected side indicating balance disorder

gait_speed.evidence: Altered gait due to balance issues

anxiety_levels.evidence: Increased anxiety due to health concerns

depression_levels.evidence: Signs of depression related to chronic condition

name: Hemolytic Uremic Syndrome
description: Hemolytic uremic syndrome (HUS) is a condition characterized by a triad of hemolytic anemia, acute renal failure, and thrombocytopenia, often triggered by infections like E. coli O157:H7.
synonyms: non-immune hemolytic anemia with acute renal failure

epidemiology.geographic_variation: High incidence in North America and Europe

pathophysiology.mechanism: Formation of platelet-fibrin thrombi in small vessels leading to hemolysis and renal impairment.
pathophysiology.molecular_basis: Shiga toxin-mediated endothelial damage.
pathophysiology.progression: Sudden onset following infectious gastroenteritis, progressing to acute renal failure.

signs.name: Oliguria
signs.description: Reduced urine output.

clinical_presentation.typical_presentation: Child with recent gastrointestinal illness, presenting with pallor, fatigue, decreased urine output, and bleeding manifestations.

diagnostic_criteria.gold_standard: Evidence of microangiopathic hemolytic anemia, renal impairment, and low platelet count.

procedural: Plasma exchange if TTP overlap suspected

special_populations.pregnancy: Avoid Eculizumab, focus on supportive care

prognosis.natural_history: Progression to renal failure without treatment
prognosis.with_treatment: Majority achieve full recovery with supportive care

warning_signs: Decreased urine output requiring immediate medical attention

rbc_count.evidence: Hemolytic anemia

platelet_count.evidence: Thrombocytopenia due to platelet consumption in thrombotic microangiopathy

hemoglobin.evidence: Hemolytic anemia causes reduced hemoglobin levels

neutrophils_absolute.evidence: Inflammatory response

lymphocytes_absolute.evidence: May vary with infectious trigger

creatinine.evidence: Acute kidney injury leading to elevated creatinine levels

bun.evidence: Renal failure leading to increased blood urea nitrogen

egfr.evidence: Reduced due to acute kidney injury

bilirubin_total.evidence: Increased due to hemolysis of red blood cells

name: Cholesteatoma
description: Cholesteatoma is an abnormal skin growth in the middle ear behind the eardrum that can lead to hearing loss and other serious complications. It is typically caused by repeated ear infections or chronic eustachian tube dysfunction.

epidemiology.age_distribution: More common in children and young adults
epidemiology.geographic_variation: Higher prevalence in low socioeconomic areas due to increased infection rates

pathophysiology.mechanism: Cholesteatoma results from eustachian tube dysfunction leading to negative pressure in the middle ear and retraction of the tympanic membrane, forming a pocket that collects keratin debris.
pathophysiology.molecular_basis: No specific genetic factors identified, but may involve inflammatory mediators and matrix metalloproteinases aiding in bone erosion.
pathophysiology.progression: Without treatment, cholesteatomas can enlarge, causing destruction of local structures, leading to hearing loss and further complications.

symptoms.name: Hearing loss
symptoms.description: Conductive hearing loss usually in the affected ear

signs.name: Retraction pocket
signs.description: Indrawn part of the tympanic membrane often filled with debris

clinical_presentation.typical_presentation: Chronic ear discharge and conductive hearing loss in a patient with a history of recurrent ear infections.

diagnostic_criteria.gold_standard: Microscopic examination and imaging

classification.criteria: Confined to the middle ear without ossicle involvement

laboratory_findings.interpretation: Degree of hearing loss and type

findings: Soft tissue mass in middle ear

additional.indication: When complications or soft tissue detail needed
findings: Differentiation of cholesteatoma from inflammatory tissue

differential_diagnosis.key_differentiator: No destructive growth or retraction pocket

prognosis.natural_history: Progressive hearing loss with potential for intracranial complications if untreated
prognosis.with_treatment: Good outcome with proper treatment though some hearing loss may persist

primary: Vaccination against pneumococcal and influenza viruses

cranial_nerves.finding: Intact II-XII, potential impairment of CN VII

name: Bipolar I Disorder
description: Bipolar I Disorder is characterized by the occurrence of at least one manic episode, often accompanied by episodes of major depression. It affects a person's mood, energy, activity levels, and the ability to carry out daily tasks.

epidemiology.age_distribution: Typical onset in late adolescence to early adulthood

pathophysiology.mechanism: Disruption in brain circuits involved in mood regulation, likely involving neurotransmitter imbalances.
pathophysiology.molecular_basis: Genetic factors linked to ion exchange processes and neurotransmitter systems.
pathophysiology.progression: Episodes can lead to progressive functional impairment if untreated.

symptoms.name: mania
symptoms.description: Elevated or irritable mood, increased activity, and risk-taking behavior

symptoms.name: major depressive episode
symptoms.description: Decreased energy, feelings of hopelessness, and anhedonia

signs.name: pressured speech
signs.description: Rapid and continuous speech pattern

clinical_presentation.typical_presentation: Manic episodes lasting at least one week, often followed or preceded by depressive episodes.

diagnostic_criteria.gold_standard: DSM-5 Criteria

classification.criteria: Elevated mood for at least one week

laboratory_findings.interpretation: R/o secondary causes of mood disorder

differential_diagnosis.key_differentiator: Duration of psychosis relative to mood symptoms

prognosis.natural_history: Recurrent episodes with potential worsening of mood stability.
prognosis.with_treatment: Improved episode control and functional recovery.

name: Vestibular Neuritis
description: Vestibular neuritis is an acute peripheral vestibulopathy characterized by the sudden onset of vertigo due to inflammation of the vestibular nerve, usually occurring after a viral infection.

epidemiology.prevalence: Uncertain, estimates around 3.5% of dizziness cases in the general population
epidemiology.mortality: Low; not typically associated with mortality

pathophysiology.mechanism: Inflammation of the vestibular nerve, often post-viral, leading to acute vestibular dysfunction without cochlear nerve involvement.
pathophysiology.molecular_basis: Possible viral reactivation affecting nerve tissue
pathophysiology.progression: Typically self-limiting over days to weeks, with gradual recovery of vestibular function.

symptoms.name: Vertigo
symptoms.description: Sudden onset of severe spinning sensation

signs.name: Spontaneous Nystagmus
signs.description: Horizontal or horizontal-rotatory nystagmus

clinical_presentation.typical_presentation: Patient often presents with sudden onset of severe vertigo, nausea, and imbalance following a recent viral illness without hearing loss.
atypical_presentations: Episode lasting only a few hours

diagnostic_criteria.gold_standard: Clinical diagnosis based on exclusion of central causes of vertigo

clinical_criteria.name: None specific
clinical_criteria.diagnosis_requires: Major criteria, absence of auditory symptoms and central signs

laboratory_findings.interpretation: Rule out bacterial infection if elevated

additional.indication: To exclude central causes of vertigo

first_line.dose: 25-50 mg PO every 6-8 hours as needed

special_populations.elderly: Monitor for increased sedation with medication

prognosis.natural_history: Most recover within weeks to months, though some residual imbalance may persist.
prognosis.with_treatment: Faster symptom relief and recovery with vestibular rehabilitation and medications.

primary: Avoidance of upper respiratory infections through vaccination
secondary: Early recognition and management of symptoms

key_points: Understanding the benign nature of the condition
Importance of completing vestibular rehabilitation exercises
warning_signs: Persistent vertigo not improving with typical course

gait.finding: Unsteady gait, veering to one side

name: Polymyositis
description: Polymyositis is an autoimmune disorder characterized by progressive symmetric proximal muscle weakness and muscle inflammation. It affects mainly the muscles closest to the trunk such as shoulder and pelvic girdle muscles.

epidemiology.geographic_variation: Higher prevalence in European and African American populations

pathophysiology.mechanism: Polymyositis involves autoimmunity against muscle fibers, leading to inflammation and muscle fiber necrosis.
pathophysiology.molecular_basis: Association with HLA-DRB1 alleles
pathophysiology.progression: Gradual onset with progressive muscle weakness and potential systemic involvement

symptoms.name: Muscle weakness
symptoms.description: Symmetric weakness primarily affecting proximal muscles

signs.name: Proximal muscle weakness
signs.description: Weakness of shoulder and hip muscles detectable on examination
signs.interpretation: Indicates possible muscle inflammation or damage

clinical_presentation.typical_presentation: Patients often present with fatigue, symmetric proximal muscle weakness, and difficulty climbing stairs or lifting arms.

diagnostic_criteria.gold_standard: Muscle biopsy showing endomysial infiltration and muscle fiber necrosis

classification.criteria: Muscle weakness with minor enzyme elevation

laboratory_findings.timing: Order when muscle weakness is noted

prognosis.natural_history: Progressive muscle weakness and potential systemic involvement
prognosis.with_treatment: Improvement in muscle strength and function

secondary: Early detection and treatment of relapses

warning_signs: Sudden increase in weakness, swallowing difficulties

esr.evidence: Elevated ESR is a marker of inflammation in polymyositis.

neutrophils_absolute.evidence: Mild increase due to inflammatory response.

ast.evidence: Muscle damage in polymyositis often leads to elevated AST levels.

alt.evidence: Muscle damage elevates liver enzymes, though ALT to a lesser extent than AST.

spo2.evidence: Potential interstitial lung disease may lower oxygen saturation.

fev1.evidence: Decreased due to potential pulmonary involvement in polymyositis.

HLA_DRB1.evidence: Associated with genetic susceptibility in polymyositis.

anti-Jo-1.evidence: Presence of anti-Jo-1 antibodies is a significant marker in polymyositis.

name: Ectopic Pregnancy
description: Ectopic pregnancy occurs when a fertilized egg implants outside the uterine cavity, most commonly in the fallopian tubes. It poses serious risks for maternal morbidity and potential mortality if untreated.

pathophysiology.mechanism: Disruption in the normal transit of a fertilized ovum through the fallopian tube leading to implantation outside the uterine cavity.
pathophysiology.molecular_basis: Alterations in tubal ciliary movement and local inflammatory processes.
pathophysiology.progression: Ectopic pregnancies may spontaneously resolve, or more commonly progress with risk of rupture leading to hemoperitoneum.

symptoms.name: amenorrhea
symptoms.description: Lack of menstrual period following a missed cycle

symptoms.name: vaginal bleeding
symptoms.description: Scant to moderate irregular vaginal bleeding

signs.name: cervical motion tenderness
signs.description: Pain elicited on cervical motion examination
signs.interpretation: Indicative of pelvic pathology such as ectopic pregnancy or pelvic inflammatory disease

signs.name: adnexal mass
signs.description: Palpable mass near the fallopian tube

clinical_presentation.typical_presentation: A woman of reproductive age presenting with lower abdominal pain, amenorrhea, and vaginal bleeding.
atypical_presentations: shoulder pain due to referred diaphragmatic pain
red_flags: severe abdominal pain with hemodynamic instability indicating potential rupture

diagnostic_criteria.gold_standard: Ultrasound with serial beta-HCG measurements

classification.criteria: Fetal pole not visible, moderate discomfort

laboratory_findings.expected_value: Suboptimal rise or plateau in beta-hCG levels
laboratory_findings.interpretation: Suggests ectopic pregnancy if levels rise <66% within 48 hours

findings: free fluid in pouch of Douglas

prognosis.natural_history: Spontaneous tubal abortion or rupture
prognosis.with_treatment: Resolution of ectopic pregnancy and preservation of fertility if early intervention occurs

secondary: early ultrasound when risk factors are present
tertiary: monitoring subsequent pregnancies in a high-risk group

name: Drowning and Nonfatal Drowning
description: Drowning refers to a respiratory impairment from submersion or immersion in liquid, potentially leading to death, morbidity, and long-term neurological consequences.

epidemiology.age_distribution: Bimodal peaks in <5 years and 15-24 years
epidemiology.geographic_variation: Higher in low to middle-income countries

pathophysiology.mechanism: Drowning leads to hypoxemia through direct lung injury involving aspiration of water, surfactant washout, and possibly pulmonary edema.
pathophysiology.molecular_basis: Disruption of alveolar-capillary membrane integrity due to fluid imbalance, contributing to acute respiratory distress.
pathophysiology.progression: Initial aspiration, followed by possible reflex laryngospasm, hypoxia, multi-organ dysfunction, and potentially fatal outcomes.

symptoms.name: respiratory distress
symptoms.description: Difficulty breathing and shortness of breath

signs.name: cyanosis
signs.description: Blue discoloration of the skin and mucous membranes
signs.technique: Examine skin and lips for color change

clinical_presentation.typical_presentation: An individual pulled from water presenting with respiratory distress or unresponsiveness.

diagnostic_criteria.gold_standard: Clinical diagnosis based on history of submersion and associated symptoms.

classification.criteria: Rescue with coughing, no resuscitation needed

laboratory_findings.interpretation: Acidosis indicates hypoxia or respiratory failure

additional.indication: Assessment of neurological sequelae or inconclusive X-ray
additional.advantages: More detailed evaluation of brain and lung

differential_diagnosis.key_differentiator: History of trauma or sepsis in ARDS without drowning

prognosis.natural_history: Rapidly progressive respiratory failure without intervention.
prognosis.with_treatment: Survival depends on duration of submersion and time to effective resuscitation.
prognosis.recurrence_rate: Depends on behavioral modification, generally preventable

key_points: Drowning can happen quickly and quietly
warning_signs: Difficulty breathing after exposure to water

resting_hr.evidence: Tachycardia is a compensatory response to hypoxia and stress.

jvp.evidence: Right heart strain due to hypoxia and cardiac compromise.

echo_ef.evidence: Cardiac function can be impaired due to direct myocardial effects and hypoxia.

wbc_count.evidence: Increased due to systemic inflammatory response to hypoxia and potential aspiration pneumonia.

hemoglobin.evidence: Dilutional effect from fluid retention and possible blood loss.

neutrophils_absolute.evidence: Neutrophilia due to stress response or secondary infection.

creatinine.evidence: Potential acute kidney injury due to hypoperfusion and hypoxia.

bun.evidence: Elevated due to renal compromise from hypoxia and hypervolemia.

sodium.evidence: Possible development of hyponatremia due to fluid overload.

potassium.evidence: Hyperkalemia from cellular damage and kidney dysfunction.

ast.evidence: Liver enzymes may rise due to hypoxic liver injury.

alt.evidence: Injury to the liver due to systemic hypoxia.

spo2.evidence: Direct hypoxia due to submersion and impaired gas exchange.

respiratory_rate.evidence: Compensatory hyperventilation in response to hypoxia.

name: Drug Overdose
description: Drug overdose is a condition resulting from the ingestion of a drug in quantities greater than are recommended or typically practiced. It can result in acute toxic effects and life-threatening symptoms requiring immediate medical intervention.

pathophysiology.mechanism: Drug overdose often results in the saturation of drug metabolizing pathways, leading to toxic accumulation and adverse effects on critical biological systems.
pathophysiology.molecular_basis: Alterations in neurotransmitter systems or direct cytotoxic effects, depending on the substance involved.
pathophysiology.progression: Symptoms typically progress rapidly, requiring prompt detection and treatment to prevent severe outcomes.

signs.name: Respiratory depression
signs.description: Reduced respiratory rate or effort.
signs.interpretation: Indicates central nervous system depressant overdose

clinical_presentation.typical_presentation: Acute onset of altered mental status and vital sign abnormalities following known or suspected excessive drug ingestion.

diagnostic_criteria.gold_standard: Plasma drug levels for specific substances

classification.criteria: Presence of toxic effects within hours of ingestion

special_populations.elderly: Adjust doses for lower renal clearance

prognosis.natural_history: Progressive worsening of symptoms can lead to organ failure and death if untreated.
prognosis.with_treatment: Most recover fully with prompt intervention; risk of long-term damage if treatment is delayed.
prognosis.recurrence_rate: 5% at 1 year with continued risk behaviors

name: Spontaneous Abortion (Miscarriage)
description: Spontaneous abortion, commonly known as miscarriage, refers to the loss of a pregnancy before 20 weeks of gestation without medical or mechanical means. It may occur due to various underlying factors, including chromosomal abnormalities and maternal health issues.

epidemiology.age_distribution: More common in women older than 35

pathophysiology.mechanism: Spontaneous loss of pregnancy due to natural causes, often related to chromosomal abnormalities or uterine issues.
pathophysiology.molecular_basis: Commonly involves chromosomal anomalies like trisomy or monosomy.
pathophysiology.progression: Typically presents with vaginal bleeding and abdominal pain, followed by expulsion of pregnancy tissue.

symptoms.name: Vaginal bleeding
symptoms.description: Bleeding that can vary from light spotting to heavy passage of blood.

symptoms.name: Abdominal pain
symptoms.description: Cramping or pain in the lower abdomen or back.

signs.name: Cervical dilation
signs.description: Cervix may be found to be dilated on examination.
signs.interpretation: Indicates impending or ongoing pregnancy loss

clinical_presentation.typical_presentation: Presentation with vaginal bleeding and cramping abdominal pain before 20 weeks of gestation.

diagnostic_criteria.gold_standard: Ultrasound confirmation of fetal loss or non-viable gestation

classification.criteria: Vaginal bleeding without cervical dilation or tissue passage

laboratory_findings.timing: At presentation and repeated to confirm trends

procedural: Dilation and curettage if tissue not expelled

prognosis.natural_history: Resolution typically occurs without intervention, future pregnancies often unaffected.
prognosis.with_treatment: Good prognosis with appropriate treatment and follow-up care.

pelvic_ultrasound.finding: No evidence of intrauterine pregnancy, possible retained products of conception

name: Henoch-Schönlein Purpura
description: Henoch-Schönlein Purpura (HSP) is a small-vessel vasculitis primarily affecting children, characterized by a purpuric rash, arthritis, abdominal pain, and renal involvement.

pathophysiology.mechanism: Immune complex deposition in small vessels, particularly IgA complexes, leading to inflammation.
pathophysiology.molecular_basis: Genetic predispositions affecting IgA handling
pathophysiology.progression: Typically self-limited, but can lead to chronic renal disease in severe cases.

symptoms.name: purpuric rash
symptoms.description: Palpable purpura primarily on buttocks and legs

symptoms.name: arthralgia
symptoms.description: Joint pain, mainly involving knees and ankles

symptoms.name: abdominal pain
symptoms.description: Colicky pain, can lead to gastrointestinal bleeding

signs.name: joint swelling
signs.description: Swelling of joints due to synovitis

signs.name: hematuria
signs.description: Microscopic or gross blood in urine

clinical_presentation.typical_presentation: Classic tetrad of palpable purpura, arthritis, abdominal pain, and renal involvement in a pediatric patient.

diagnostic_criteria.gold_standard: Clinical diagnosis based on symptom constellation

classification.criteria: initial skin purpura without renal involvement

special_populations.pregnancy: No specific precautions required due to typical pediatric population
special_populations.renal_impairment: Dose adjustment if significant renal involvement

prognosis.natural_history: Usually self-limited, resolves within weeks
prognosis.with_treatment: Good prognosis, reduced symptom severity and duration
prognosis.recurrence_rate: 33% with full resolution, especially in first year

key_points: Monitor for changes in urine color
Seek care for severe abdominal pain

wbc_count.evidence: Mild leukocytosis due to inflammation

platelet_count.evidence: Reactive thrombocytosis in response to systemic inflammation

esr.evidence: Elevated due to systemic inflammation and vasculitis

neutrophils_absolute.evidence: Neutrophilia can be present in response to inflammation

lymphocytes_absolute.evidence: Relative lymphopenia observed in acute inflammatory states

creatinine.evidence: Possible renal involvement with nephritis can lead to decreased kidney function

bun.evidence: Renal impairment in Henoch-Schönlein Purpura increases BUN

egfr.evidence: Reduced due to glomerulonephritis affecting kidney filtering efficiency

respiratory_rate.evidence: Potential respiratory symptom exacerbation leads to increased respiratory rate

iga_deposition.evidence: IgA deposition in small vessels is a hallmark of the disease

heart_sounds.finding: Normal S1 and S2, no murmurs

edema.finding: Mild pitting edema in lower extremities

name: Preeclampsia
description: Preeclampsia is a pregnancy-specific syndrome characterized by new-onset hypertension and proteinuria, occurring after 20 weeks gestation. It poses significant risks for both mother and fetus, including potential progression to eclampsia.

pathophysiology.mechanism: Inadequate placentation leads to reduced placental perfusion and placental ischemia, which in turn triggers endothelial dysfunction, vasoconstriction, and hypertension.
pathophysiology.molecular_basis: Imbalance in angiogenic factors such as increased soluble fms-like tyrosine kinase-1 (sFlt-1) and reduced placental growth factor (PlGF).
pathophysiology.progression: Progresses from mild to severe, potentially leading to eclampsia, HELLP syndrome, and multiorgan failure.

signs.name: Hypertension
signs.description: Blood pressure ≥140/90 mmHg

signs.name: Proteinuria
signs.description: ≥0.3 g/24 hours or protein/creatinine ratio ≥0.3

clinical_presentation.typical_presentation: A pregnant woman after 20 weeks of gestation presenting with hypertension and significant proteinuria.
atypical_presentations: elevated liver enzymes with low platelets

diagnostic_criteria.gold_standard: Clinical diagnosis based on ACOG guidelines

classification.criteria: BP ≥160/110 mmHg with target organ dysfunction

differential_diagnosis.key_differentiator: History of hypertension prior to pregnancy

adjunctive.dose: 4-6 g IV loading dose, then 1-2 g/hr

special_populations.pregnancy: Initiate treatment based on clinical features and trimester

prognosis.natural_history: Without intervention, progresses to eclampsia or HELLP syndrome.
prognosis.with_treatment: Improved maternal and fetal outcomes; reduced risk of complications.

unfavorable: Severe preeclampsia at early gestational age

key_points: Report headache or visual changes immediately
lifestyle_modifications: Emphasize rest and limited physical activity

name: Intussusception
description: Intussusception is a condition where a part of the intestine telescopes into an adjacent segment, leading to bowel obstruction. It's most common in infants and young children.

epidemiology.prevalence: 1-4 per 1000 cases in pediatric acute abdomen

pathophysiology.mechanism: Telescoping of a proximal bowel segment into a distal segment leading to obstruction and ischemia.
pathophysiology.molecular_basis: Linked with Peyer's patches hypertrophy post viral infection.
pathophysiology.progression: May lead to bowel ischemia, necrosis, or perforation if untreated.

symptoms.name: abdominal pain
symptoms.description: Severe, colicky pain with episodes of crying and lethargy

symptoms.name: bloody stool
symptoms.description: Currant jelly-like stools due to blood and mucus

signs.name: sausage-shaped abdominal mass
signs.description: Palpable mass in the right hypochondrium or mid-abdomen

clinical_presentation.typical_presentation: Infant with intermittent severe abdominal pain, vomiting, and currant jelly stools.
red_flags: sudden onset abdominal pain in an infant

diagnostic_criteria.gold_standard: Ultrasound showing target or doughnut sign

findings: Lack of gas in the colon

differential_diagnosis.key_differentiator: CT or ultrasound findings specific for appendicitis

surgical: Surgical reduction or resection if enema fails

prognosis.natural_history: May lead to bowel ischemia, necrosis, or perforation if untreated.
prognosis.with_treatment: Excellent with timely intervention; most children recover fully.

key_points: Sudden abdominal pain in children requires immediate medical attention

resting_hr.evidence: Pain and potential dehydration can cause increased heart rate.

wbc_count.evidence: Inflammatory response due to bowel obstruction or compromise.

hemoglobin.evidence: Potential bleeding may lead to slight anemia.

creatinine.evidence: Dehydration can lead to elevated creatinine levels.

bun.evidence: Dehydration often results in increased BUN levels.

respiratory_rate.evidence: Pain and anxiety from the condition can lead to increased respiratory rate.

abdominal_exam.finding: Palpable abdominal mass, right lower quadrant

relevant_genes.description: Gene expression changes related to acute inflammatory response

name: Eclampsia
description: Eclampsia is a severe complication of preeclampsia, characterized by the onset of seizures in a pregnant woman with no prior history of a seizure disorder. It is a medical emergency requiring immediate attention.

epidemiology.prevalence: approx. 2% of pregnancies complicated by preeclampsia
epidemiology.age_distribution: Typically in reproductive age women 20-35 years
epidemiology.sex_ratio: F:M is N/A since it affects only pregnant individuals

pathophysiology.mechanism: Believed to result from cerebral vasospasm and over-perfusion of microvascular beds leading to cerebral edema and seizures.
pathophysiology.molecular_basis: Dysregulation of the vascular endothelial growth factors, contributing to endothelial dysfunction.
pathophysiology.progression: Pre-eclamptic features progress to central nervous system involvement with the occurrence of seizures.

signs.name: hypertension
signs.description: blood pressure >140/90 mmHg

signs.name: edema
signs.description: peripheral swelling

clinical_presentation.typical_presentation: Pregnant woman with pre-existing preeclampsia presenting with generalized seizures and hypertension.
red_flags: new-onset seizures during pregnancy—urgent medical evaluation required

diagnostic_criteria.gold_standard: Clinical diagnosis based on the presence of seizures in a woman with preeclampsia

clinical_criteria.name: No specific criteria
clinical_criteria.diagnosis_requires: Presence of seizures in the context of preeclampsia

classification.description: Eclampsia is a singular definable event

additional.indication: If CT is inconclusive or for detailed brain assessment

differential_diagnosis.key_differentiator: Seizures present without hypertensive disorder history

first_line.dose: 4-6 g IV bolus, then 1-2 g/hour IV infusion

adjunctive.dose: 20 mg IV initial dose, then titrate
adjunctive.monitoring: Monitor blood pressure and heart rate

prognosis.natural_history: Rapid deterioration without treatment leading to maternal and fetal complications
prognosis.with_treatment: Good outcomes with proper management
prognosis.recurrence_rate: Significant risk in future pregnancies without prophylaxis

secondary: Close monitoring in women with preeclampsia

name: Hypertrophic Pyloric Stenosis
description: Hypertrophic pyloric stenosis is a condition in infancy where the pyloric muscle thickens, causing gastric outlet obstruction. It leads to severe projectile vomiting and requires surgical intervention.

epidemiology.age_distribution: Typically presents at 3-12 weeks of age

pathophysiology.mechanism: Progressive hypertrophy and hyperplasia of the pyloric muscle leading to gastric outlet obstruction.
pathophysiology.molecular_basis: Potential genetic predisposition; no specific genes identified.
pathophysiology.progression: Progressively worsens without intervention leading to dehydration and electrolyte imbalances.

symptoms.name: Projectile vomiting
symptoms.description: Forceful vomiting that occurs shortly after feeding

symptoms.name: Poor weight gain
symptoms.description: Failure to thrive due to vomiting

signs.name: Palpable olive
signs.description: Pyloric mass felt in the right upper quadrant
signs.technique: Palpation of the abdomen above the umbilicus after vomiting

signs.name: Visible peristalsis
signs.description: Wave-like movements across the abdomen
signs.technique: Observation of the abdomen while the infant is calm

clinical_presentation.typical_presentation: An infant aged 3-5 weeks presenting with projectile vomiting and palpable gastric mass.

diagnostic_criteria.gold_standard: Ultrasound showing pyloric muscle hypertrophy

procedural: Endoscopic balloon dilation if surgical options are limited

prognosis.natural_history: Progressive worsening of symptoms leading to severe dehydration and nutritional deficits
prognosis.with_treatment: Excellent outcome with surgery and supportive care

irritability.evidence: Discomfort due to hunger and dehydration

name: HELLP Syndrome
description: HELLP syndrome is an obstetric complication characterized by hemolysis, elevated liver enzymes, and low platelet count, usually considered a variant of preeclampsia and can be life-threatening for both the mother and the fetus.
synonyms: hemolysis elevated liver enzymes low platelets

epidemiology.age_distribution: Primarily affects women of reproductive age
epidemiology.geographic_variation: More common in high-risk pregnant populations

pathophysiology.mechanism: The syndrome results from endothelial dysfunction and microvascular thrombosis, leading to hemolysis, liver dysfunction, and thrombocytopenia.
pathophysiology.molecular_basis: Platelet activation and aggregation with coagulation pathway activation.
pathophysiology.progression: Rapid onset typically in the last trimester, can worsen quickly without intervention.

symptoms.name: epigastric or right upper quadrant pain
symptoms.description: Sharp or dull pain near the liver

signs.name: elevated blood pressure
signs.description: Blood pressure >140/90 mmHg

clinical_presentation.typical_presentation: Pregnant female >20 weeks gestation with high blood pressure, right upper quadrant pain, nausea, and malaise.
red_flags: severe epigastric pain and altered mental status

diagnostic_criteria.gold_standard: No single test; diagnosis is clinical with lab confirmation

first_line.dose: 4-6 g IV loading dose, then 2 g/hr

prognosis.natural_history: Progressive if untreated with risk of complications like hepatic rupture
prognosis.with_treatment: Good if promptly treated with delivery of fetus

key_points: Seek early medical advice if symptoms develop

name: Gestational Diabetes Mellitus
description: Gestational diabetes mellitus is a type of diabetes characterized by high blood glucose levels discovered during pregnancy in women who were not previously diagnosed with diabetes. It can pose risks to both the mother and developing fetus if not managed effectively.

epidemiology.mortality: Low if managed, but complications can increase morbidity
epidemiology.geographic_variation: Higher prevalence in South Asian, Black, Middle Eastern populations

pathophysiology.mechanism: Insulin resistance increases during pregnancy due to placental hormone release, leading to glucose intolerance.
pathophysiology.molecular_basis: Involves the presence of placental hormones such as human placental lactogen.
pathophysiology.progression: Develops typically in the second trimester; resolves post-partum but increases future type 2 diabetes risk.

signs.name: Polyuria
signs.description: Increased urinary frequency

clinical_presentation.typical_presentation: Frequently detected during routine prenatal screenings as hyperglycemia without specific complaints.

diagnostic_criteria.gold_standard: Oral Glucose Tolerance Test (OGTT) with specific thresholds

clinical_criteria.name: ADA Criteria (American Diabetes Association)
clinical_criteria.diagnosis_requires: Any one of the major criteria

classification.criteria: Abnormal glucose tolerance identified in the second trimester

first_line.dose: Dose individualized based on glucose levels

prognosis.natural_history: Resolves postpartum but increases risk of future diabetes.
prognosis.with_treatment: Good with management; most achieve normal outcomes.

survival_rates.5_year: Risk of developing type 2 diabetes post pregnancy
survival_rates.10_year: Higher risk of developing type 2 diabetes

warning_signs: Persistent hyperglycemia symptoms requiring immediate care

name: Placenta Previa
description: Placenta previa is a condition during pregnancy where the placenta partially or completely covers the cervix, leading to a risk of severe bleeding before or during delivery.

epidemiology.mortality: Rare, but severe complications can lead to maternal or fetal mortality

pathophysiology.mechanism: The placenta implants in the lower uterine segment, potentially covering the cervical os.
pathophysiology.molecular_basis: No specific genetic factors identified
pathophysiology.progression: May resolve with uterine growth, but can lead to bleeding in later pregnancy stages if unresolved.

symptoms.name: Painless vaginal bleeding
symptoms.description: Sudden, painless vaginal bleeding in the second or third trimester.

signs.name: Visible external os covered by placenta
signs.description: On speculum examination, cervix cannot be visualized clearly due to obstruction by the placenta.

clinical_presentation.typical_presentation: Painless bleeding in the third trimester with a confirmed lower placental position on ultrasound
red_flags: Heavy bleeding requiring immediate medical attention

diagnostic_criteria.gold_standard: Transvaginal ultrasound showing placenta covering the internal cervical os in the third trimester

classification.criteria: Placenta near but not covering the os
Placenta reaching the margin of the os

laboratory_findings.expected_value: Low hemoglobin if bleeding has occurred
laboratory_findings.timing: On presentation and after any bleeding episode

distinguishing_features: Fetal blood vessels cross or run near the internal os
differential_diagnosis.key_differentiator: Presence of fetal vessels near os

first_line.dose: Betamethasone 12 mg IM every 24 hours for 2 doses
first_line.duration: Immediate administration if preterm labor risks

special_populations.hepatic_impairment: Caution with medications metabolized by liver

prognosis.natural_history: Potential for spontaneous resolution as pregnancy progresses
prognosis.with_treatment: Good outcomes with planned C-section and medical management

warning_signs: Sudden vaginal bleeding requiring immediate medical evaluation

hemoglobin.evidence: Maternal blood volume increase and dilution

platelet_count.evidence: Dilution due to increased plasma volume

bnp.evidence: Heart strain due to increased preload

placental_location.value: Low-lying or entirely covering cervical os

name: Placental Abruption
description: Placental abruption is the premature separation of the placenta from the uterus, a serious complication during pregnancy that can lead to significant maternal and fetal morbidity and mortality.

pathophysiology.mechanism: Bleeding between the uterine wall and placenta causes separation, disrupting blood flow to the fetus.
pathophysiology.molecular_basis: No specific genetic markers
pathophysiology.progression: Can progress rapidly leading to fetal distress, maternal hemorrhage, and coagulopathy

symptoms.name: vaginal bleeding
symptoms.description: Acute onset of bleeding, may vary in amount

symptoms.name: abdominal pain
symptoms.description: Severe, sudden onset abdominal or back pain

signs.name: uterine tenderness
signs.description: Hypertonic and painful on palpation

signs.name: fetal distress
signs.description: Abnormal fetal heart rate patterns

clinical_presentation.typical_presentation: Sudden-onset vaginal bleeding and abdominal pain in third-trimester pregnant woman.

diagnostic_criteria.gold_standard: Clinical diagnosis confirmed by ultrasound

classification.criteria: Minor vaginal bleeding, stable vital signs

differential_diagnosis.key_differentiator: Ultrasound shows placental location over cervix

distinguishing_features: sudden severe pain, ruptured uterus on ultrasound

goals: Delivery if fetal or maternal indications

first_line.dose: 12 mg IM every 24 hours for 2 doses

special_populations.pregnancy: Betamethasone if less than 34 weeks gestation

prognosis.natural_history: Spontaneous resolution is rare; may progress to fetal distress and maternal instability
prognosis.with_treatment: Improved maternal and fetal outcomes with timely intervention

secondary: Regular prenatal visits for early detection

name: Postpartum Hemorrhage
description: Postpartum hemorrhage is defined as a significant blood loss occurring after childbirth. It is a leading cause of maternal morbidity and mortality worldwide, requiring prompt diagnosis and management.

protective_factors: active management of third stage of labor

pathophysiology.mechanism: The primary mechanism is uterine atony, where the uterus fails to contract effectively after delivery leading to excessive blood loss.
pathophysiology.molecular_basis: No specific molecular markers identified.
pathophysiology.progression: If not interventioned, it can lead to hypovolemic shock and maternal death.

symptoms.name: excessive bleeding
symptoms.description: Bleeding more than 500 ml after vaginal birth or over 1000 ml after cesarean section within 24 hours.

signs.name: hypotension
signs.description: Low blood pressure observed in severe cases of postpartum hemorrhage.
signs.technique: Measure blood pressure using a sphygmomanometer.
signs.interpretation: Indicates severe blood loss and possible shock.

clinical_presentation.typical_presentation: A patient presents with heavy vaginal bleeding shortly after delivery along with signs of hypovolemia.
red_flags: continued severe bleeding despite uterotonic use

diagnostic_criteria.gold_standard: Clinical diagnosis based on visual estimation and patient symptoms.

clinical_criteria.name: WHO Definitions
major_criteria: Blood loss > 500 ml after vaginal delivery
Blood loss > 1000 ml after cesarean section

laboratory_findings.interpretation: Indicates anemia due to blood loss.

additional.indication: Persistent bleeding and suspicion of uterine rupture.

differential_diagnosis.key_differentiator: Characteristic atonic, boggy uterus on examination.

first_line.monitoring: Monitor blood pressure and uterine tone.

procedural: balloon tamponade if refractory to medication

special_populations.pregnancy: Not applicable as PPH occurs post-delivery
special_populations.hepatic_impairment: Cautious use of certain drugs metabolized by liver

prognosis.natural_history: Without treatment, can progress to severe morbidity or mortality due to hypovolemic shock.
prognosis.with_treatment: Good outcomes with prompt and effective management.

primary: active management of third stage of labor

systolic_bp.evidence: Hypotensive response due to blood loss

bnp.evidence: Cardiac strain due to fluid overload

name: Hyperemesis Gravidarum
description: Hyperemesis gravidarum is a severe form of nausea and vomiting in pregnancy that can lead to dehydration, electrolyte imbalance, and significant weight loss. It typically occurs in the first trimester and requires aggressive management to ensure maternal and fetal well-being.

pathophysiology.mechanism: It is believed to be caused by hormonal changes, including elevated levels of hCG and estrogen, leading to gastrointestinal dysmotility.
pathophysiology.molecular_basis: Genetic predisposition has been suggested involving genes related to hormone metabolism.
pathophysiology.progression: Without treatment, it can progress to severe dehydration and malnutrition, but usually improves after the first trimester.

symptoms.name: severe nausea
symptoms.description: Unremitting nausea that is more persistent and severe than typical morning sickness

symptoms.name: vomiting
symptoms.description: Frequent, excessive vomiting leading to fluid loss

signs.name: dehydration
signs.description: Dry mucous membranes, decreased skin turgor
signs.technique: Physical examination for skin turgor and mucous membranes

signs.name: weight loss
signs.description: Weight loss >5% of pre-pregnancy weight

clinical_presentation.typical_presentation: A pregnant woman in the first trimester presenting with intractable nausea, frequent vomiting, weight loss, and signs of dehydration.
atypical_presentations: symptoms persisting into the second trimester
may present with jaundice or ketosis
red_flags: signs of severe dehydration or electrolyte imbalance requiring hospitalization

diagnostic_criteria.gold_standard: Clinical diagnosis based on history and symptoms

classification.criteria: Nausea without vomiting or moderate vomiting with no weight loss

laboratory_findings.timing: At diagnosis and regularly during treatment

findings: Normal, rule out multiple gestation or molar pregnancy

additional.indication: Consider in atypical cases or unclear diagnosis

first_line.monitoring: Monitor maternal weight and fetal growth

special_populations.renal_impairment: Modify doses based on renal function
special_populations.hepatic_impairment: Use caution with hepatically metabolized drugs

prognosis.natural_history: Symptoms usually resolve by mid-pregnancy (20 weeks)
prognosis.with_treatment: Most women improve significantly with treatment

secondary: Early identification and management of symptoms

warning_signs: Severe dehydration signs requiring immediate medical attention

name: Preterm Labor
description: Preterm labor is defined as regular uterine contractions accompanied by cervical changes that occur before 37 weeks of gestation. It is a leading cause of neonatal morbidity and mortality.

epidemiology.mortality: 10% neonatal mortality in extremely preterm infants
epidemiology.geographic_variation: Higher prevalence in sub-Saharan Africa, South Asia

pathophysiology.mechanism: Preterm labor results from hormonal, mechanical, or inflammatory triggers that lead to cervical effacement, and uterine contractions.
pathophysiology.molecular_basis: Involves prostaglandin production and progesterone withdrawal.
pathophysiology.progression: If untreated, progresses from cervical dilation to the delivery of the fetus.

symptoms.name: Uterine contractions
symptoms.description: Regular contractions occurring more than once every 10 minutes

symptoms.name: Pelvic pressure
symptoms.description: Feeling of pressure in the pelvis

signs.name: Cervical dilation
signs.description: Dilation of the cervix beyond 2 centimeters

clinical_presentation.typical_presentation: Pregnant woman under 37 weeks of gestation experiencing regular and frequent uterine contractions with cervical changes.
red_flags: significant cervical change over short period

diagnostic_criteria.gold_standard: Regular uterine contractions and cervical changes before 37 weeks of gestation

laboratory_findings.interpretation: Presence increases risk of preterm birth

additional.advantages: No radiation, detailed soft tissue imaging

first_line.dose: 30 mg PO loading, then 10-20 mg PO every 4-6 hours

special_populations.pregnancy: Nifedipine as first choice, avoid NSAIDs
special_populations.renal_impairment: Dose adjustments as needed based on renal function

prognosis.natural_history: Progression to delivery if untreated, with risk of neonatal complications like respiratory distress syndrome.
prognosis.with_treatment: Improved fetal outcomes and delayed delivery

primary: Screening and early intervention for risk factors
secondary: Routine cervical length screening in at-risk populations
tertiary: Retraining pre-prematue labor guidelines for resulting complications

key_points: Awareness of signs of preterm labor

name: Age-Related Macular Degeneration
description: Age-related macular degeneration (AMD) is a leading cause of vision loss in the elderly, characterized by progressive damage to the macula of the retina. It is divided into dry (atrophic) and wet (neovascular) forms, with the latter associated with more severe visual impairment.

protective_factors: Diet high in fruits and vegetables

pathophysiology.mechanism: AMD results from the accumulation of drusen and subsequent retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) dysfunction and photoreceptor degeneration.
pathophysiology.molecular_basis: Involvement of the complement pathway, specifically CFH gene variants.
pathophysiology.progression: Begins with asymptomatic drusen deposits, progressing to geographic atrophy and/or choroidal neovascularization in advanced stages.

signs.name: Drusen
signs.description: Yellow deposits under the retina

clinical_presentation.typical_presentation: Elderly patient presenting with gradual central vision loss and distortion, characterized by drusen on fundoscopic examination.
atypical_presentations: Rapid onset of severe vision loss due to choroidal neovascularization
red_flags: Sudden severe visual loss, indicative of retinal detachment or neovascular AMD

diagnostic_criteria.gold_standard: Optical coherence tomography (OCT) and fundus fluorescein angiography

laboratory_findings.timing: Consider in family history of AMD

prognosis.natural_history: Progressive vision loss in advanced stages.
prognosis.with_treatment: Stabilization or improvement with anti-VEGF injections.

primary: Diet rich in fruits and vegetables

warning_signs: Sudden vision changes requiring immediate evaluation

fundoscopy.finding: Drusen and retinal pigment epithelium changes

relevant_genes.description: Gene expression changes specific to macular degeneration progression

name: Mastoiditis
description: Mastoiditis is an infection of the mastoid bone of the skull, typically following acute otitis media. It can lead to serious complications if untreated.

epidemiology.prevalence: 0.05-0.1% of patients with acute otitis media

pathophysiology.mechanism: Infection spreads from the middle ear to the mastoid air cells, leading to inflammation and possible abscess formation.
pathophysiology.molecular_basis: Bacterial pathogens such as Streptococcus pneumoniae, Haemophilus influenzae
pathophysiology.progression: May progress to mastoid abscess or intracranial complications if untreated.

symptoms.name: Ear pain
symptoms.description: Severe, persistent pain behind the ear

signs.name: Postauricular swelling
signs.description: Swelling behind the ear

signs.name: Otorrhea
signs.description: Discharge from the ear

clinical_presentation.typical_presentation: Child with acute history of otitis media presenting with fever, ear pain, and postauricular swelling.

diagnostic_criteria.gold_standard: CT scan of temporal bones showing destruction of mastoid air cells

first_line.dose: 45-90 mg/kg PO daily in divided doses

procedural: Myringotomy if middle ear fluid persists
surgical: Mastoidectomy if abscess or lack of response to treatment

prognosis.natural_history: May progress to chronic infection or intracranial extension
prognosis.with_treatment: Good outcomes with prompt treatment

primary: Vaccination against Haemophilus influenzae and Streptococcus pneumoniae

motor_exam.finding: Mild weakness in right upper limb

sensory_exam.finding: Decreased sensation in right upper limb

cranial_nerves.finding: Deficit in facial nerve (VII) on right side

ct_head.finding: Mastoid air cells opacification, possible temporal bone involvement

mri_brain.finding: Inflammation and possible abscess formation in the cerebellopontine angle

name: Premature Rupture of Membranes
description: Premature rupture of membranes (PROM) is characterized by the rupture of the fetal membranes before the onset of labor. It occurs when the amniotic sac breaks, leading to leakage of amniotic fluid.

epidemiology.mortality: Increased risk for infant and maternal morbidity and mortality
epidemiology.age_distribution: More common in teens and late reproductive age

pathophysiology.mechanism: Weakening of the amniotic sac membrane due to inflammation, infection, or biochemical factors.
pathophysiology.molecular_basis: Involvement of matrix metalloproteinases causing degradation of collagen.
pathophysiology.progression: Can lead to premature labor if not managed; risk of infection increases significantly as duration extends.

symptoms.name: Vaginal fluid leakage
symptoms.description: Sudden gush or steady trickle of fluid from the vagina.

signs.name: Pooling of fluid
signs.description: Visual confirmation of amniotic fluid in the vaginal posterior fornix during speculum examination.

clinical_presentation.typical_presentation: Pregnant woman at any gestational age presenting with complaints of fluid leaking from the vagina.

diagnostic_criteria.gold_standard: Amnisure or ROM Plus tests confirming amniotic fluid proteins.

distinguishing_features: Often thicker and not associated with labor signs

first_line.dose: 12 mg IM every 24 hours for 2 doses

procedural: Amniocentesis if necessary for fetal lung maturity

special_populations.pregnancy: Use corticosteroids to promote fetal lung maturity in preterm cases

prognosis.natural_history: Without intervention, risk of chorioamnionitis and premature labor.
prognosis.with_treatment: Improved neonatal outcomes with timely intervention.

survival_rates.1_year: Varies with gestational age at ROM

name: Chorioamnionitis
description: Chorioamnionitis is an infection of the fetal membranes (amnion and chorion) typically caused by bacterial infiltration that can occur before or during labor. It is a significant cause of maternal and neonatal morbidity.

protective_factors: Prophylactic antibiotics during labor with premature rupture of membranes

pathophysiology.mechanism: Bacteria ascends from the vaginal flora causing inflammation and infection in the fetal membranes.
pathophysiology.molecular_basis: Common pathogens include E. coli, Group B Streptococcus, and Mycoplasma species.
pathophysiology.progression: Inflammation leads to increased uterine activity, preterm labor, and can progress to fetal infection.

signs.name: Maternal tachycardia
signs.description: Elevated maternal heart rate

signs.name: Fetal tachycardia
signs.description: Elevated fetal heart rate over 160 bpm

clinical_presentation.typical_presentation: Fever, uterine tenderness, maternal and/or fetal tachycardia, and purulent amniotic fluid.
atypical_presentations: No fever but with clinical signs

diagnostic_criteria.gold_standard: Cultures of amniotic fluid showing bacterial growth

classification.criteria: Fever and tachycardia without membrane rupture

special_populations.pregnancy: Antibiotic regimen must be safe for the fetus
special_populations.hepatic_impairment: Monitor liver function if on multiple medications

prognosis.natural_history: Progressive infection leading to complications like sepsis if untreated
prognosis.with_treatment: High recovery rate with prompt antibiotic treatment

primary: Antibiotic prophylaxis for preterm premature rupture of membranes

confusion.evidence: Altered mental status due to infection

name: Intrauterine Growth Restriction
description: Intrauterine Growth Restriction (IUGR) refers to a condition where a fetus is smaller than expected for the number of weeks of pregnancy and is not growing at a normal rate inside the womb. It is associated with increased risks of perinatal morbidity and mortality.

epidemiology.incidence: Varies with population and criteria used
epidemiology.mortality: Increased perinatal mortality, specific percentage varies
epidemiology.age_distribution: Primarily affects pregnancies at any maternal age

pathophysiology.mechanism: Impaired placental perfusion and function lead to inadequate fetal nutrient and oxygen supply, restricting fetal growth.
pathophysiology.molecular_basis: No specific genetic abnormalities are consistently identified.
pathophysiology.progression: Progressive with potential for increased fetal stress and hypoxia as pregnancy advances.

signs.name: Small symphysis-fundal height
signs.description: Measurement below the gestational age norm
signs.technique: Measure from the pubic symphysis to the top of the uterus

clinical_presentation.typical_presentation: Antenatal finding of fundal height lagging by 2 or more weeks.

diagnostic_criteria.gold_standard: Serial ultrasound biometry

clinical_criteria.name: Ultrasound-based criteria
major_criteria: Estimated fetal weight below the 10th percentile for gestational age

laboratory_findings.expected_value: Increased resistance or absent/reversed end-diastolic flow

additional.indication: Complex cases or when ultrasound is inconclusive

special_populations.renal_impairment: Adjust medications with renal dosing considerations

prognosis.natural_history: Risk of stillbirth, preterm birth, and neonatal complications without intervention
prognosis.with_treatment: Improved survival with close monitoring and timely delivery

survival_rates.5_year: Similar to general population if no neonatal sequelae
survival_rates.10_year: Long-term outcomes depend on underlying causes

tertiary: Follow-up care for preterm birth complications

doppler_ultrasound.finding: Absent or reversed end-diastolic flow in umbilical artery

bnp.evidence: Heart strain due to placental insufficiency

name: Postpartum Depression
description: Postpartum depression is a severe form of clinical depression occurring shortly after childbirth, typically within the first four weeks postpartum. It is characterized by a persistent low mood, high levels of anxiety, and difficulty bonding with the newborn.

pathophysiology.mechanism: Hormonal changes postpartum, including drops in estrogen and progesterone, affect mood regulation pathways.
pathophysiology.molecular_basis: Changes in serotonin and norepinephrine levels
pathophysiology.progression: Can develop into chronic depression if untreated

symptoms.name: Persistent low mood
symptoms.description: Feeling down most of the day

signs.name: Flat affect
signs.description: Limited emotional expression

clinical_presentation.typical_presentation: New mother experiencing persistent sadness, lack of energy, difficulty sleeping, and anxiety about the wellbeing of her baby.

diagnostic_criteria.gold_standard: Clinical interview by a mental health professional using DSM-5 criteria

clinical_criteria.name: DSM-5 Criteria for Major Depressive Episode
clinical_criteria.diagnosis_requires: 5 or more symptoms for at least 2 weeks

laboratory_findings.expected_value: Possible atypical results if thyroid disorder coexists
laboratory_findings.interpretation: Rule out thyroid dysfunction as secondary cause

goals: Ensure safety of mother and baby

special_populations.pregnancy: Breastfeeding mothers need dose adjustments and monitoring

prognosis.natural_history: Can persist and worsen without treatment
prognosis.with_treatment: Good prognosis with appropriate therapy

primary: Scheduled mental health screenings during pregnancy

relevant_genes.description: Altered expression of genes related to mood regulation

appetite.evidence: Loss of appetite due to depressive symptoms

progesterone.evidence: Influence of stress on reproductive axis

name: Neonatal Respiratory Distress Syndrome
description: Neonatal Respiratory Distress Syndrome, also known as hyaline membrane disease, is a condition predominantly seen in preterm neonates due to surfactant deficiency. It is characterized by respiratory difficulty shortly after birth.

epidemiology.incidence: 1% of term infants and up to 50% of preterm infants
epidemiology.geographic_variation: Higher in regions with limited neonatal intensive care

pathophysiology.mechanism: Surfactant deficiency leads to alveolar collapse, decreased lung compliance, and impaired gas exchange.
pathophysiology.molecular_basis: Surfactant comprises lipids and proteins critical for reducing alveolar surface tension.
pathophysiology.progression: Rapid onset of respiratory distress post-birth, typically worsens over 48-72 hours and gradually improves with surfactant production or treatment.

signs.name: Grunting
signs.description: Expiratory sound due to partial closure of the glottis

clinical_presentation.typical_presentation: Preterm infant with tachypnea, nasal flaring, and grunting soon after birth.
red_flags: Cyanosis not relieved by oxygen supplementation

diagnostic_criteria.gold_standard: Clinical diagnosis supported by chest X-ray findings

laboratory_findings.timing: Within first few hours of life

procedural: Intubation and mechanical ventilation if necessary

prognosis.natural_history: Majority improve with supportive care; risk of chronic lung disease if untreated
prognosis.with_treatment: Significantly improved with surfactant therapy

primary: Antenatal corticosteroids to mothers at risk of preterm delivery
secondary: Early identification and management in at-risk neonates
tertiary: Management of complications like bronchopulmonary dysplasia

warning_signs: Cyanosis and grunting requiring immediate attention

respiratory_rate.evidence: Increased effort due to respiratory distress

chest_xray.evidence: Typical for Neonatal Respiratory Distress Syndrome

systolic_bp.evidence: Transient hypertension in response to hypoxia

name: Neonatal Jaundice
description: Neonatal jaundice is characterized by elevated bilirubin levels in the blood, leading to yellowing of the skin and eyes in newborns. It is common, typically benign, but requires monitoring to prevent kernicterus, a form of brain damage.

epidemiology.mortality: Low, but kernicterus carries a significant risk
epidemiology.age_distribution: Typically occurs within the first week of life
epidemiology.geographic_variation: Higher prevalence in East Asian populations

pathophysiology.mechanism: Increased bilirubin production from hemolysis, decreased clearance due to immature liver function.
pathophysiology.molecular_basis: Deficient UDP-glucuronosyltransferase activity.
pathophysiology.progression: Can progress to kernicterus if untreated in severe cases.

symptoms.name: yellowing of the skin and eyes

signs.name: jaundice visible above the diaphragm
signs.description: Yellow discoloration visible on the forehead, chest, or back on physical examination

clinical_presentation.typical_presentation: A newborn appears yellow in the face and upper body within the first 3-5 days of life.

diagnostic_criteria.gold_standard: Serum bilirubin level measurement

clinical_criteria.name: AAP 2023 Guidelines
major_criteria: Total serum bilirubin exceeding 95th percentile for age in hours

special_populations.renal_impairment: Reduce dose of medication if applicable
special_populations.hepatic_impairment: Caution with medications metabolized by liver

prognosis.natural_history: Most cases resolve spontaneously without intervention
prognosis.with_treatment: Excellent if treated promptly

secondary: Regular screening in the first few days

epidemiology.incidence: 6-10% in very low birth weight infants

pathophysiology.molecular_basis: Altered gut microbiota composition, immature immune response in preterm neonates.
pathophysiology.progression: Initial vascular compromise and mucosal injury, followed by bacterial invasion, leading to systemic sepsis and shock if untreated.

name: Intraventricular Hemorrhage in Newborn
description: Intraventricular hemorrhage (IVH) in newborns is a condition where there is bleeding into the brain's ventricular system. It is most common in premature infants due to immature cerebral vasculature and complications associated with prematurity.

pathophysiology.mechanism: Due to fragile and immature blood vessels in the germinal matrix that can rupture, leading to bleeding into the ventricular system.
pathophysiology.molecular_basis: Involves immature autoregulation of cerebral blood flow leading to fluctuation in cerebral perfusion pressure.
pathophysiology.progression: Ranges from minimal bleeding (Grade I) to severe bleeding with ventricular dilation (Grades III-IV), sometimes progressing to post-hemorrhagic ventricular dilation.

name: Retinopathy of Prematurity
description: Retinopathy of prematurity (ROP) is a potentially blinding eye disorder primarily affecting premature infants, characterized by abnormal retinal blood vessel development. Its severity can range from mild with spontaneous resolution to severe with significant visual impairment.

epidemiology.age_distribution: Preterm infants, particularly those < 32 weeks gestation
epidemiology.geographic_variation: Higher prevalence in regions with advanced neonatal care

pathophysiology.mechanism: Disorder in retinal vascular development due to premature birth and exposure to fluctuating oxygen levels.
pathophysiology.molecular_basis: Involves factors like vascular endothelial growth factor (VEGF).
pathophysiology.progression: From avascular retina leading to neovascularization and possibly retinal detachment.

name: Bronchopulmonary Dysplasia
description: Bronchopulmonary Dysplasia (BPD) is a chronic lung disease primarily affecting premature infants who require mechanical ventilation and oxygen therapy. It is characterized by inflammation and scarring in the lungs.

epidemiology.prevalence: 30% in very low birth weight infants
epidemiology.incidence: Varies based on region and medical care access
epidemiology.mortality: 10-20% depending on severity and healthcare access
epidemiology.age_distribution: Primarily affects neonates, particularly preterm infants born before 28 weeks
epidemiology.geographic_variation: Higher incidence in regions with limited access to advanced neonatal care

pathophysiology.mechanism: Chronic inflammation and scarring due to mechanical ventilation and oxygen therapy leading to arrested alveolar development.
pathophysiology.molecular_basis: Role of inflammation, cytokine release, oxidative stress and impaired growth factor signaling.
pathophysiology.progression: Starts with oxygen and ventilation therapy in preterm infants, progressing to chronic lung disease marked by reduced alveolarization and lung function.

name: Meconium Aspiration Syndrome
description: Meconium Aspiration Syndrome (MAS) is a condition in newborns caused by the inhalation of meconium-stained amniotic fluid, leading to respiratory distress and potentially severe pulmonary complications.
synonyms: Neonatal respiratory distress due to meconium

pathophysiology.mechanism: Inhalation of meconium-stained amniotic fluid causes airway obstruction, chemical pneumonitis, and surfactant dysfunction.
pathophysiology.molecular_basis: No known genetic basis.
pathophysiology.progression: Symptoms often present immediately after birth, with potential for rapid deterioration.

name: Transient Tachypnea of the Newborn
description: Transient Tachypnea of the Newborn (TTN) is a respiratory condition characterized by rapid breathing in the early hours of life due to delayed clearance of fetal lung fluid. It is often self-limiting and presents mainly in term or near-term infants.

epidemiology.age_distribution: Neonates, especially within the first 24-72 hours of life

pathophysiology.mechanism: TTN occurs due to delayed clearance of fetal lung fluid, which results in pulmonary edema and subsequent respiratory distress.
pathophysiology.molecular_basis: No specific molecular or genetic factors identified.
pathophysiology.progression: TTN typically resolves within 12 to 72 hours as lung fluid is absorbed.

pathophysiology.progression: Progressive and chronic with increasing pain and potential infertility over time.
