signs.name: clue cells
signs.description: epithelial cells covered in bacteria viewed under microscope
signs.technique: Microscopic examination of wet mount smear

clinical_presentation.typical_presentation: A woman presenting with a thin, grayish discharge and fishy odor

diagnostic_criteria.gold_standard: Amsel's criteria or Gram stain

prognosis.natural_history: May resolve spontaneously, but often recurs
prognosis.with_treatment: High success rate, but recurrence is possible

warning_signs: return of odor or discharge requiring attention

name: Erectile Dysfunction
description: Erectile Dysfunction (ED) is the persistent inability to achieve or maintain an erection sufficient for satisfactory sexual performance. It can be an indicator of underlying health problems including cardiovascular or psychological conditions.

epidemiology.geographic_variation: Higher prevalence reported in Western countries

pathophysiology.mechanism: Reduced blood flow to the penis due to vascular, neurogenic, or psychological factors.
pathophysiology.molecular_basis: Involvement of nitric oxide pathways affecting blood flow.
pathophysiology.progression: Can progress and worsen over time if underlying risk factors are not managed.

symptoms.name: Inability to maintain erection
symptoms.description: Difficulty in maintaining an erection suitable for intercourse.

signs.name: Decreased penile rigidity
signs.description: Noted upon physical examination.
signs.interpretation: Indicative of vascular or neurogenic dysfunction

clinical_presentation.typical_presentation: A middle-aged or older male reporting persistent difficulties in achieving or maintaining an erection.
atypical_presentations: Men without any apparent risk factors
red_flags: Sudden onset ED associated with pelvic trauma

diagnostic_criteria.gold_standard: Detailed sexual history and physical examination.

clinical_criteria.name: DSM-5 Criteria
major_criteria: Presence of symptoms for at least 6 months
minor_criteria: Not better explained by other disorders

prognosis.natural_history: May progress without intervention.
prognosis.with_treatment: Significant improvement in most cases with appropriate management.

warning_signs: Sudden onset could indicate other medical issues

name: Testicular Torsion
description: Testicular torsion is a urological emergency characterized by the twisting of the spermatic cord, resulting in reduced blood flow to the testicle, which can lead to ischemia and potentially testicular loss if not treated promptly.

epidemiology.mortality: Low, but high risk of testicular loss without urgent treatment
epidemiology.age_distribution: Most common in adolescents aged 12-18 years
epidemiology.sex_ratio: M:F ratio not applicable, affects males only

pathophysiology.mechanism: Twisting of the spermatic cord cuts off the venous drainage and eventually the arterial inflow, leading to testicular ischemia.
pathophysiology.molecular_basis: No specific genetic mutations identified, but familial tendency noted.
pathophysiology.progression: If untreated, may lead to necrosis and loss of the testicle within 6-12 hours.

symptoms.name: Acute scrotal pain
symptoms.description: Sudden onset of severe pain in one testicle

signs.name: High-riding testis
signs.description: Affected testicle appears to be higher or closer to the pubic bone
signs.technique: Visual inspection and palpation of the scrotum

signs.name: Absent cremasteric reflex
signs.description: No elevation of the testicle when stroking the inner thigh
signs.technique: Elicit reflex via gentle stimulation of the inner thigh

clinical_presentation.typical_presentation: Sudden onset of severe unilateral testicular pain with nausea and vomiting in a young adolescent male.
red_flags: Acute, severe testicular pain with nausea and vomiting

diagnostic_criteria.gold_standard: Surgical exploration for definitive diagnosis

classification.criteria: Mild pain with preserved testicular blood flow

findings: Decreased or absent blood flow to testicle

differential_diagnosis.key_differentiator: Presence of increased blood flow on Doppler ultrasound
Ultrasound confirming normal testicular blood flow

procedural: Manual detorsion if delay in surgery

special_populations.elderly: Standard approach but consider comorbid conditions
special_populations.renal_impairment: Dosage adjustments for medication as necessary
special_populations.hepatic_impairment: Dosage adjustments for medication as necessary

monitoring: Follow-up ultrasound to confirm testicular flow

prognosis.natural_history: Testicular necrosis within 6-12 hours if untreated
prognosis.with_treatment: Excellent if surgery within 6 hours; testicular preservation rate >90%
prognosis.recurrence_rate: Low after orchidopexy on both testes

primary: Awareness of testicular pain as an emergency

key_points: Seek immediate medical attention for acute testicular pain
Testicular torsion is a surgical emergency
lifestyle_modifications: Avoid activities that can lead to scrotal trauma
warning_signs: Sudden severe testicular pain, nausea, and vomiting

heart_rate.evidence: Tachycardia due to pain and stress

hemoglobin.evidence: Anemia due to acute disease state

doppler_ultrasound.finding: Reduced or absent blood flow to affected testis

blood_flow.evidence: Reduced or absent blood flow to the affected testis

name: Epididymitis
description: Epididymitis is the inflammation of the epididymis, commonly due to bacterial infection and presents with scrotal pain and swelling. It is frequently associated with urinary tract infections and sexually transmitted infections.

epidemiology.incidence: Approximately 600,000 cases per year in the USA
epidemiology.mortality: Low, mortality not significant if treated
epidemiology.geographic_variation: Higher incidence in areas with high STD prevalence

pathophysiology.mechanism: Retrograde flow of infected urine into the epididymis from the urethra and the ejaculatory duct.
pathophysiology.molecular_basis: Bacterial infections often involve E. coli or sexually transmitted pathogens like Chlamydia trachomatis.
pathophysiology.progression: If untreated, can lead to chronic pain or infertility.

symptoms.name: scrotal pain
symptoms.description: Acute onset of pain, often unilateral

signs.name: Prehn's sign
signs.description: Elevation of the scrotum relieves pain

signs.name: epididymal tenderness
signs.description: Tenderness on palpation of the epididymis

clinical_presentation.typical_presentation: Sudden onset of scrotal pain and swelling, often with fever and dysuria.
red_flags: suspicion of testicular torsion requiring immediate urological emergency management

diagnostic_criteria.gold_standard: Urine culture and positive nucleic acid amplification test for STIs

differential_diagnosis.key_differentiator: Doppler ultrasound showing decreased blood flow

special_populations.pregnancy: Adapt treatment to partner for STI

prognosis.natural_history: Progression to chronic pain or infertility if untreated.
prognosis.with_treatment: Excellent with appropriate antibiotics, symptoms resolve in days to weeks

secondary: prompt treatment of urinary tract infections

warning_signs: Severe worsening pain requiring immediate medical evaluation

name: Testicular Cancer
description: Testicular cancer is a type of cancer that originates in the germ cells of the testicles. It commonly affects younger men, typically between the ages of 15 and 35, and is highly treatable with good prognosis if detected early.

pathophysiology.mechanism: Malignant transformation of germ cells in the testis
pathophysiology.molecular_basis: Genetic mutations such as alterations in the KIT gene
pathophysiology.progression: Invasion into local structures and potential metastasis to lymph nodes and distant organs

symptoms.name: testicular pain
symptoms.description: Dull ache or sharp pain in the scrotum

signs.name: testicular mass on palpation
signs.description: Detectable hard or irregular mass in one testicle
signs.technique: Use both hands to palpate each testicle gently

clinical_presentation.typical_presentation: Painless enlargement of the testicle in a young male

diagnostic_criteria.gold_standard: Histological examination post orchidectomy

first_line.duration: 5 days per cycle, repeat every 3 weeks

prognosis.natural_history: May metastasize to lymph nodes, lungs
prognosis.with_treatment: Most patients cured

warning_signs: new mass or swelling in the testicle

scrotal_exam.finding: Palpable, firm, non-tender mass in right testicle

relevant_genes.description: Gene expression changes specific to testicular germ cell tumors

name: Urinary Incontinence
description: Urinary incontinence is the involuntary loss of urine, which can result from a variety of underlying conditions affecting the bladder, urethra, or nervous system. It significantly impacts quality of life and can lead to social or hygiene issues.

epidemiology.incidence: variable depending on age and sex
epidemiology.mortality: low directly, but associated with increased mortality due to falls in the elderly

pathophysiology.mechanism: Urinary incontinence can result from detrusor overactivity, sphincter weakness, or neurological impairment, leading to involuntary urine loss.
pathophysiology.molecular_basis: In some cases, alterations in cholinergic receptors or pelvic floor collagen may contribute.
pathophysiology.progression: Without treatment, symptoms can worsen, particularly stress incontinence and detrusor overactivity.

signs.name: Urine leakage during cough
signs.description: Observed leakage during stress maneuvers like coughing

clinical_presentation.typical_presentation: Involuntary loss of urine during activities like coughing, sneezing, or physical exertion.

diagnostic_criteria.gold_standard: Urodynamic testing

prognosis.natural_history: Progressive worsening without intervention
prognosis.with_treatment: Improved control and quality of life

progesterone.evidence: Hormonal balance related to bladder control

name: Interstitial Cystitis
description: Interstitial cystitis, also known as painful bladder syndrome, is a chronic condition characterized by bladder pressure, bladder pain, and sometimes pelvic pain. Its etiology is unclear, but it is thought to involve multiple factors, including inflammation, defects in the bladder tissue, and possibly autoimmune mechanisms.

epidemiology.geographic_variation: More common in North America and Europe

pathophysiology.mechanism: Not fully understood; potential involvement of bladder mucosa defects, mast cell activation, and neurogenic inflammation.
pathophysiology.molecular_basis: Aberrant expression of urothelial growth factors and cytokines.
pathophysiology.progression: Chronic condition that can have remissions and exacerbations.

symptoms.name: pelvic pain
symptoms.description: Pain in lower abdomen or pelvic area

symptoms.name: increased urinary frequency
symptoms.description: Need to urinate frequently during the day and night

signs.name: suprapubic tenderness
signs.description: Tenderness upon palpation of the lower abdomen
signs.technique: Palpate the lower abdomen with gentle pressure

clinical_presentation.typical_presentation: Chronic pelvic pain and urinary frequency, often with suprapubic tenderness on examination.
red_flags: sudden onset of severe pelvic pain

diagnostic_criteria.gold_standard: Cystoscopic examination with hydrodistention showing glomerulations or Hunner's lesions

clinical_criteria.name: American Urological Association Criteria
clinical_criteria.diagnosis_requires: Both major + at least one minor

additional.indication: Complex cases or to rule out other conditions

prognosis.natural_history: Chronic with intermittent flare-ups
prognosis.with_treatment: Improved symptoms and quality of life

name: Contact Dermatitis
description: Contact dermatitis is an inflammatory condition of the skin resulting from exposure to allergens or irritants, leading to erythema, itching, and vesiculation. It can be classified into allergic contact dermatitis, a delayed hypersensitivity reaction, and irritant contact dermatitis, which is a non-immune response.

epidemiology.geographic_variation: Higher prevalence in occupations with chemical exposure

pathophysiology.mechanism: Allergic contact dermatitis occurs due to a type IV hypersensitivity reaction where lymphocytes recognize allergens and trigger an immune response, while irritant contact dermatitis results from direct cytotoxic effects on the skin cells.
pathophysiology.molecular_basis: Involvement of cytokines like IL-2, IL-4 in allergic processes;
pathophysiology.progression: From initial erythema and edema to vesiculation and lichenification with chronicity.

symptoms.name: Itching (pruritus)
symptoms.description: Persistent or intense itching at affected site

symptoms.name: Erythema
symptoms.description: Redness of the skin due to increased blood flow

signs.name: Vesiculation
signs.description: Formation of small blisters

clinical_presentation.typical_presentation: Patient presents with itching and erythematous rash at site of contact with specific irritant or allergen.
atypical_presentations: Eczematous plaques distant from exposure site

diagnostic_criteria.gold_standard: Patch testing for allergens

laboratory_findings.interpretation: Identifies trigger allergens for allergic dermatitis

differential_diagnosis.key_differentiator: Chronicity and lack of clear contact trigger

prognosis.natural_history: Resolution within weeks upon avoidance.
prognosis.with_treatment: Rapid improvement with medical therapy.

name: Seborrheic Dermatitis
description: Seborrheic dermatitis is a chronic inflammatory dermatologic condition that primarily affects areas rich in sebaceous glands like the scalp, face, and upper trunk. It presents as scaly, erythematous patches and may be associated with pruritus.

pathophysiology.mechanism: Malassezia yeast colonization, immune response causing inflammation, and hyperproliferation of the epidermis.
pathophysiology.molecular_basis: Role of Malassezia species in altering skin lipids leading to inflammation
pathophysiology.progression: Chronic, recurrent course with flare-ups

symptoms.name: Scalp flaking
symptoms.description: Flaky, itchy white to yellowish scales on scalp

signs.name: Erythematous plaques
signs.description: Red, inflamed plaques with greasy scales

clinical_presentation.typical_presentation: Greasy scales on erythematous skin located in scalp, nasolabial folds, and eyebrows
red_flags: Severe, widespread rash in immunocompromised suggests an opportunistic infection

diagnostic_criteria.gold_standard: Clinical diagnosis based on appearance and location of lesions

laboratory_findings.expected_value: Higher colonies count in affected areas

special_populations.elderly: Monitor for skin thinning with steroids

prognosis.natural_history: Chronic with intermittent flare-ups; can improve with age.
prognosis.with_treatment: Good control with treatment, symptoms often improve significantly.

secondary: Regular monitoring and early treatment of flare-ups

immune_response.description: Possible alterations in systemic inflammatory markers, although typically minimal

itchiness.description: Pruritus is often associated, especially on the scalp

relevant_genes.description: Genetic predispositions may include variations in genes related to immune response and skin barrier function

name: Acne Vulgaris
description: Acne vulgaris is a chronic inflammatory skin condition that affects the pilosebaceous units and primarily affects adolescents. It is characterized by areas of seborrhea, comedones, papules, nodules, and possible scarring.

epidemiology.sex_ratio: 1:1, slight male predominance in severe cases

pathophysiology.mechanism: Increased sebum production, follicular hyperkeratinization, colonization by Cutibacterium acnes, and inflammation.
pathophysiology.molecular_basis: Involvement of androgens increasing sebum production; inflammatory response to Cutibacterium acnes.
pathophysiology.progression: Typically starts in adolescence, can persist into adulthood with varying degrees of severity.

symptoms.name: Comedones
symptoms.description: Non-inflammatory lesions consisting of open and closed comedones.

signs.name: Papules and Pustules
signs.description: Inflammatory lesions characterized by small red bumps and pus-filled lesions.

clinical_presentation.typical_presentation: Adolescent with facial, back, and chest papules, pustules, and comedones.
red_flags: sudden severe outbreak, indication of endocrinopathy

diagnostic_criteria.gold_standard: Clinical examination and history

laboratory_findings.interpretation: Useful in cases of suspected endocrinopathy
laboratory_findings.timing: Consider in severe cases or atypical presentation

special_populations.hepatic_impairment: Monitor liver function with systemic retinoids

prognosis.natural_history: Resolution of symptoms over time, with potential for persistence into adulthood.
prognosis.with_treatment: Significant reduction in lesion count and improvement in quality of life.

anxiety_level.evidence: Emotional distress related to skin condition

name: Rosacea
description: Rosacea is a chronic inflammatory skin condition characterized by facial erythema, papules, pustules, and vascular manifestations primarily affecting the central face. It often worsens with triggers like sun exposure, hot drinks, and stress.

epidemiology.incidence: Varies widely; higher in fair-skinned individuals

pathophysiology.mechanism: Vascular dysregulation and inflammatory responses leading to chronic facial erythema and telangiectasia.
pathophysiology.molecular_basis: Potential role of cathelicidin peptides and toll-like receptor dysregulation.
pathophysiology.progression: Early vascular changes progress to inflammatory lesions and possible ocular involvement.

symptoms.name: Facial erythema
symptoms.description: Persistent redness, particularly on central face

symptoms.name: Papules and pustules
symptoms.description: Red bumps and pus-filled lesions over cheeks, nose, and forehead

signs.name: Telangiectasia
signs.description: Visible small, dilated blood vessels on the face

clinical_presentation.typical_presentation: Patient with persistent facial redness, periodic flushing, and inflammatory lesions over cheeks and nose.
red_flags: Sudden vision changes (indicating potential ocular rosacea)

diagnostic_criteria.gold_standard: Clinical diagnosis based on history and examination

clinical_criteria.name: Standard Criteria for Diagnosis of Rosacea

differential_diagnosis.key_differentiator: Rash in the malar area without papules/pustules

prognosis.natural_history: May fluctuate with periods of improvement and exacerbation.
prognosis.with_treatment: Most patients achieve control of symptoms with appropriate therapy.
prognosis.recurrence_rate: Variable, often correlates with management compliance

warning_signs: Sudden vision changes or eye irritation

name: Vitiligo
description: Vitiligo is an acquired chronic depigmentation disorder characterized by the loss of functional melanocytes in the skin, leading to well-demarcated white patches. It is associated with significant psychological impacts due to its visible manifestations.

epidemiology.age_distribution: Commonly begins in second to third decade

pathophysiology.mechanism: Autoimmune destruction of melanocytes, genetic susceptibilities, and environmental triggers.
pathophysiology.molecular_basis: Associated with genes like NLRP1 and PTPN22
pathophysiology.progression: Progressive course with periods of stability and exacerbation.

signs.name: Koebner phenomenon
signs.description: Lesions appearing at sites of trauma

clinical_presentation.typical_presentation: Symmetrical white patches, often around the eyes, mouth, and on the hands and feet.
red_flags: Rapidly progressive lesions with associated soreness

diagnostic_criteria.gold_standard: Clinical diagnosis, Wood's lamp examination for confirmation

laboratory_findings.expected_value: Normal unless autoimmune thyroid disease is present

additional.limitations: Less effective for very light skin tones

differential_diagnosis.key_differentiator: Pityriasis alba patches are not completely depigmented

special_populations.renal_impairment: Dose adjustment unnecessary for topical treatments
special_populations.hepatic_impairment: Dose adjustment unnecessary for topical treatments

monitoring: Monitor for adverse effects of treatment

prognosis.natural_history: Progressive with potential for periods of remission and exacerbation.
prognosis.with_treatment: Improvement in pigmentation and cosmetic appearance.

secondary: Annual thyroid function screening in individuals with vitiligo

key_points: Regular use of sunscreen is important
warning_signs: Rapid spread of lesions, especially with soreness or itching

lesions.finding: Symmetrical hypopigmented macules on extremities and face

wood_lamp.finding: Bright blue-white fluorescence of affected areas

name: Alopecia Areata
description: Alopecia Areata is an autoimmune disorder characterized by patchy hair loss on the scalp, face, and sometimes other areas of the body. It occurs when the immune system mistakenly attacks hair follicles, leading to hair loss.

pathophysiology.mechanism: Immune-mediated damage to hair follicles due to autoreactive T-cells.
pathophysiology.molecular_basis: Gene associations include HLA-DR/DQ, AIRE, and PTPN22.
pathophysiology.progression: May progress from patchy hair loss to complete hair loss over affected areas.

symptoms.name: Patchy Hair Loss
symptoms.description: Circumscribed areas of hair loss on the scalp or other body parts.

signs.name: Exclamation Mark Hairs
signs.description: Short hairs that taper and lose pigment near the base.
signs.technique: Scalp examination using a handheld magnifying lens
signs.interpretation: Indicative of active hair follicle inflammation

clinical_presentation.typical_presentation: Sudden onset of round or oval patches of hair loss primarily on the scalp.
atypical_presentations: Ophiasis pattern, with hair loss around the scalp edges
Sisaipho pattern, with hair loss sparing scalp edges

diagnostic_criteria.gold_standard: Clinical examination and exclusion of other causes of hair loss

laboratory_findings.expected_value: Normal in alopecia areata unless thyroid disease coexists

prognosis.natural_history: May resolve spontaneously, recur, or persist.
prognosis.with_treatment: Improves hair regrowth outcomes; frequent relapses.

hemoglobin.evidence: Related to stress or dietary deficiency

lesion.description: Discrete patches of complete hair loss

name: Urticaria (Hives)
description: Urticaria, commonly known as hives, is a skin condition characterized by the rapid appearance of red, itchy welts. These are often transient and caused by dermal mast cell activation and histamine release.

epidemiology.age_distribution: Can occur at any age but peaks in adults 20-40 years

pathophysiology.mechanism: Urticaria results from mast cell and basophil degranulation, releasing histamine and other mediators, leading to increased vascular permeability and dermal edema.
pathophysiology.molecular_basis: IgE-mediated pathways and non-IgE mechanisms
pathophysiology.progression: Typically acute, self-limiting; chronic forms may persist beyond 6 weeks

symptoms.name: Itching
symptoms.description: Intense itching typically preceding the appearance of welts

symptoms.name: Welts
symptoms.description: Raised red or skin-colored welts with well-defined edges that appear and disappear quickly

signs.name: Dermatographism
signs.description: Inflammatory wheal formation on stroking of the skin
signs.technique: Gently stroke skin with a blunt object

clinical_presentation.typical_presentation: Acute onset of intensely itchy, evanescent weals lasting less than 24 hours

diagnostic_criteria.gold_standard: Clinical evaluation based on symptomatology

laboratory_findings.interpretation: May suggest an underlying infection if abnormal

special_populations.elderly: Use lower doses due to potential for increased sedation
special_populations.hepatic_impairment: Monitor liver function with long-term corticosteroids

prognosis.natural_history: Most cases resolve spontaneously
prognosis.with_treatment: Rapid symptom relief with antihistamines

relevant_genes.description: Gene expression changes associated with acute urticaria

name: Impetigo
description: Impetigo is a highly contagious superficial skin infection, most commonly affecting children, characterized by pustules and honey-colored crusted erosions.

pathophysiology.mechanism: Infection caused mainly by Staphylococcus aureus or Group A Streptococcus.
pathophysiology.molecular_basis: Superficial invasion of epidermis by bacteria.
pathophysiology.progression: Can spread through autoinoculation or close contact.

signs.name: Honey-colored crusts
signs.description: Yellowish crusts over ruptured pustules

clinical_presentation.typical_presentation: Erythematous macules progress to vesicles and rupture, forming honey-colored crusts primarily on the face and extremities.

diagnostic_criteria.gold_standard: Clinical diagnosis based on appearance and history

laboratory_findings.expected_value: Isolation of S. aureus or Streptococcus pyogenes

special_populations.pregnancy: Limited systemic antibiotics due to safety concerns
special_populations.elderly: Standard dosing with renal adjustment if needed
special_populations.hepatic_impairment: Monitor liver function with systemic antibiotics

prognosis.natural_history: Typically self-limiting but may cause complications if untreated
prognosis.with_treatment: Excellent prognosis with rapid resolution
prognosis.recurrence_rate: Variable, depends on hygiene and environmental factors

secondary: Monitoring for early detection in contacts

warning_signs: Fever or spreading redness in affected area

lesions.finding: Honey-colored crusted lesions on face and extremities

bacterial_culture.result: Positive for Staphylococcus aureus or Streptococcus pyogenes

relevant_genes.description: Gene expression changes associated with inflammatory response in impetigo

name: Urticaria (Hives)
description: Urticaria, commonly known as hives, is a skin condition characterized by transient, erythematous, and often itchy wheals of varying sizes. It can be acute or chronic in nature, triggered by allergenic substances or other factors.

epidemiology.mortality: Rare, primarily in cases associated with anaphylaxis
epidemiology.age_distribution: All age groups with peak at 20-40 years

pathophysiology.mechanism: Localized mast cell degranulation and release of histamine and other vasoactive substances leading to increased vascular permeability.
pathophysiology.molecular_basis: Histamine release from basophils and mast cells, triggered by allergens, stress, or idiopathic reasons.
pathophysiology.progression: Acute urticaria resolves within 6 weeks; chronic may persist for more than 6 weeks.

symptoms.name: Itchy wheals
symptoms.description: Raised, erythematous plaques with central pallor and pruritus

signs.name: Dermatographism
signs.description: Exaggerated wealing when the skin is stroked
signs.technique: Stroke the skin with a blunt object

clinical_presentation.typical_presentation: Sudden onset of itchy raised red or skin-colored welts of varying size across the skin.

diagnostic_criteria.gold_standard: Clinical evaluation based on history and presentation; skin prick tests for specific allergens

clinical_criteria.name: Clinical Criteria for Urticaria
minor_criteria: duration less than or more than 6 weeks

laboratory_findings.expected_value: Eosinophilia in cases of allergic reactions
laboratory_findings.interpretation: Eosinophilia can indicate an allergic component

special_populations.elderly: Start at lower doses of antihistamines

prognosis.natural_history: May resolve spontaneously, especially in acute cases
prognosis.with_treatment: Improved symptom control and decreased frequency

key_points: Urticaria can be managed with lifestyle modifications.

name: Scabies
description: Scabies is a contagious skin infestation caused by the mite Sarcoptes scabiei, characterized by intense itching and a pimple-like skin rash. It is transmitted through close physical contact and commonly affects crowded living situations.

epidemiology.age_distribution: all ages, more common in young children
epidemiology.geographic_variation: higher rates in tropical and subtropical regions
protective_factors: reducing close contact with affected individuals

pathophysiology.mechanism: Sarcoptes scabiei burrows into the skin, causing intense itching through allergic sensitization and inflammatory response.
pathophysiology.molecular_basis: No specific genetic factors identified, related to immune response to mite proteins.
pathophysiology.progression: Without treatment, mites continue to reproduce, causing widespread infestation and secondary infections.

signs.name: burrow
signs.description: thin, grayish-white line on skin

clinical_presentation.typical_presentation: Intense itching and a pimple-like rash, with burrows typically on the wrists, elbows, armpits, belt line, and webs of fingers.
red_flags: widespread crusting and severe itching in immunocompromised hosts

diagnostic_criteria.gold_standard: Identification of mites, eggs, or feces from skin scrapings under a microscope

laboratory_findings.expected_value: Presence of mites, eggs, or feces

non_pharmacological: Wash all textiles in hot water

first_line.duration: Single application, repeated in 1 week if necessary

special_populations.pregnancy: Use topical treatments; avoid oral ivermectin
special_populations.elderly: Standard treatment, monitor for skin irritation

prognosis.natural_history: Untreated, infestation persists and may spread to others
prognosis.with_treatment: Excellent response, symptoms typically resolve within weeks

key_points: Scabies is not due to poor hygiene but is very contagious.
All household members should be treated.

skin_scraping.finding: Mite, egg, or fecal pellet identified

appetite.evidence: Reduced food intake due to discomfort

name: Stevens-Johnson Syndrome
description: Stevens-Johnson Syndrome (SJS) is a severe mucocutaneous reaction, typically to medication or infection, characterized by widespread epidermal necrosis and sloughing of the dermis. It is life-threatening due to associated complications such as infections and organ failure.

epidemiology.age_distribution: Primarily affects young adults, but can occur at any age

pathophysiology.mechanism: Immune-mediated hypersensitivity response leading to keratinocyte apoptosis and detachment at the dermal-epidermal junction.
pathophysiology.molecular_basis: Involvement of Fas-FasL pathway and other apoptosis-inducing factors.
pathophysiology.progression: Rapid onset of symptoms progressing to extensive skin and mucosal detachment.

symptoms.name: skin rash
symptoms.description: widespread erythematous or purpuric macules that progress to blisters and sloughing

symptoms.name: mucosal involvement
symptoms.description: painful erosions of oral, ocular, and genital mucosa

signs.name: Nikolsky sign
signs.description: slight rubbing of the skin results in exfoliation of the outermost layer
signs.technique: Apply lateral pressure to the skin

signs.name: Target lesions
signs.description: Characteristic skin lesions with three concentric zones of color

clinical_presentation.typical_presentation: Patient presents with fever, malaise, and rash that rapidly progresses to blistering and sloughing, affecting <10% of body surface area.

diagnostic_criteria.gold_standard: Histopathology showing epidermal apoptosis and necrosis

clinical_criteria.name: SCORTEN score
clinical_criteria.diagnosis_requires: Presence of characteristic rash and mucosal involvement

laboratory_findings.interpretation: May indicate infection or stress response

special_populations.renal_impairment: Adjust medications based on renal function

prognosis.natural_history: Can progress rapidly to involve multiple organ systems without treatment
prognosis.with_treatment: Improved outcomes with early intervention

survival_rates.1_year: Survival depends on acute phase management

physical_exam.finding: Widespread purpuric macules, which coalesce into large blisters, especially on trunk and face

name: Toxic Epidermal Necrolysis
description: Toxic Epidermal Necrolysis (TEN) is a severe skin condition characterized by widespread erythema, necrosis, and detachment of the epidermis and mucous membranes, leading to a risk of serious complications due to skin barrier loss.

pathophysiology.mechanism: Drug-induced cytotoxic reaction resulting in widespread keratinocyte apoptosis mediated by activated T cells and cytokines.
pathophysiology.molecular_basis: Associations with HLA alleles like HLA-B*1502.
pathophysiology.progression: Rapid progression from erythema and blistering to widespread skin sloughing.

symptoms.name: fever
symptoms.description: High-grade fever often preceding skin lesions

signs.name: Nikolsky's sign
signs.description: Positive when slight rubbing results in exfoliation of the outermost layer
signs.technique: Apply lateral pressure to the skin

signs.name: Mucosal involvement
signs.description: Blistering and erosions on mucous membranes
signs.technique: Inspect oral, ocular, and genital mucosa
signs.interpretation: Significant mucosal damage often accompanies TEN

clinical_presentation.typical_presentation: Sudden onset of fever and malaise followed by erythematous and blistering skin lesions, rapidly evolving to widespread epidermal detachment.
red_flags: systemic symptoms such as fever and respiratory distress

diagnostic_criteria.gold_standard: Skin biopsy showing full-thickness epidermal necrosis

classification.criteria: Mild skin involvement without extensive sloughing

laboratory_findings.interpretation: Liver involvement due to systemic reaction

differential_diagnosis.key_differentiator: Extent of body surface area involvement

procedural: Intensive care unit support if needed

special_populations.renal_impairment: Dose adjustments for renally cleared drugs

prognosis.natural_history: Rapid progression with high risk of complications if untreated
prognosis.with_treatment: Improved survival with early intervention and supportive care

name: Herniated Intervertebral Disc
description: A herniated disc occurs when the soft center of a spinal disc pushes through a crack in the tougher exterior casing, possibly compressing spinal nerves and causing pain.

pathophysiology.mechanism: Disc degeneration or trauma results in disc material protruding into the spinal canal, often compressing nerves.
pathophysiology.molecular_basis: Age-related changes in collagen content and water retention in the disc.
pathophysiology.progression: May lead to chronic pain, numbness, or weakness if untreated.

symptoms.name: Radicular pain
symptoms.description: Sharp or burning pain radiating down the leg, usually unilateral

signs.name: Straight Leg Raise Test
signs.description: Pain radiating down the leg when the straightened leg is raised
signs.technique: Raise the leg with knee extended, patient supine
signs.interpretation: Indicative of lumbosacral nerve root irritation

clinical_presentation.typical_presentation: Patients often present with lower back pain radiating down the leg, sometimes accompanied by sensory or motor deficits.

name: Spinal Stenosis
description: Spinal stenosis is a condition characterized by narrowing of the spinal canal, which may lead to compression of the nerve roots or spinal cord. It most commonly occurs in the lumbar and cervical regions, causing symptoms ranging from pain to neurological deficits.

pathophysiology.mechanism: Degenerative changes such as osteophyte formation, disc herniation, and ligament thickening lead to narrowing of the spinal canal.
pathophysiology.molecular_basis: Associated with degenerative changes and biomechanical stress altering spinal anatomy.
pathophysiology.progression: Starts with mild back pain to severe neurological symptoms as compression worsens.

symptoms.name: Neurogenic claudication
symptoms.description: Pain, numbness, or weakness in legs increased with walking and relieved by sitting or bending forward.

signs.name: Romberg's sign
signs.description: Stability worsens when eyes closed due to proprioceptive loss.
signs.technique: Patient stands with feet together and eyes closed.
signs.interpretation: Indicates proprioceptive or spinal cord dysfunction.

clinical_presentation.typical_presentation: Gradual onset of lower back pain with leg pain during walking, relieved by sitting.
red_flags: loss of bowel or bladder control

diagnostic_criteria.gold_standard: MRI showing narrowing of the spinal canal with nerve compression

classification.criteria: Mild symptoms with normal daily function

distinguishing_features: pain does not relieve immediately by sitting

prognosis.natural_history: Progresses slowly, with intermittent periods of stability.
prognosis.with_treatment: Symptoms can significantly improve with proper intervention.

warning_signs: notify doctor of sudden increased pain or weakness

mri.finding: Narrowing of spinal canal at L4-L5, L5-S1 with nerve root compression

reflex_testing.evidence: L4/L5 reflex testing shows diminished responses

name: Rotator Cuff Tear
description: A rotator cuff tear is a tear of one or more of the tendons or muscles of the rotator cuff of the shoulder, commonly affecting the supraspinatus tendon. It may occur due to acute injury or degenerative changes over time.

epidemiology.age_distribution: Increases with age, common in elderly

pathophysiology.mechanism: Tendinopathy due to overload or trauma leading to tear, mostly in the supraspinatus tendon.
pathophysiology.molecular_basis: Matrix metalloproteinases upregulation leading to collagen breakdown
pathophysiology.progression: Without intervention, can progress to full-thickness tear or massive cuff tear.

clinical_criteria.name: American Academy of Orthopaedic Surgeons criteria

differential_diagnosis.key_differentiator: Impingement tests positive, no tear on imaging

prognosis.natural_history: Can lead to degenerative changes if untreated
prognosis.with_treatment: Excellent with early intervention

warning_signs: Sudden worsening of pain or function

mri.finding: Full-thickness tear of the supraspinatus tendon

sensory_testing.finding: Intact except reduced sensation over deltoid

name: Frozen Shoulder
description: Frozen shoulder, or adhesive capsulitis, is a condition characterized by stiffness and pain in the shoulder joint that gradually worsens over time. It typically involves inflammation and thickening of the shoulder capsule, leading to limited range of motion.

epidemiology.age_distribution: Most common in individuals aged 40-60 years

pathophysiology.mechanism: The condition is characterized by inflammation and fibrosis of the shoulder joint capsule, resulting in pain and decreased range of motion.
pathophysiology.molecular_basis: Possible involvement of inflammatory cytokines and joint capsule constriction
pathophysiology.progression: Typically progresses through three stages: freezing (pain and motion limitation), frozen (stiffness without pain), and thawing (gradual return of motion).

range_of_motion.finding: Severely limited external rotation and abduction

mri.finding: Capsular thickening consistent with adhesive capsulitis

name: Plantar Fasciitis
description: Plantar fasciitis is a common condition that causes pain in the heel and bottom of the foot. It occurs due to inflammation of the plantar fascia, a thick band of tissue that connects the heel bone to the toes.

epidemiology.incidence: estimated 1 million cases per year in the US

pathophysiology.mechanism: Chronic overload and microtrauma lead to the inflammation and degeneration of the plantar fascia.
pathophysiology.molecular_basis: Involves inflammatory cytokines and matrix metalloproteinases.
pathophysiology.progression: Typically resolves over time with self-care; may become chronic in some cases.

prognosis.with_treatment: Symptom improvement expected within weeks to months.

name: Tendinitis
description: Tendinitis is an inflammatory condition of the tendon usually caused by overuse or repetitive injury. It is characterized by pain at the tendon site and may result in functional impairment.

pathophysiology.mechanism: Degenerative changes in the tendon often due to chronic overload or acute injury leading to inflammation.
pathophysiology.molecular_basis: Alteration in collagen structure and matrix degradation.
pathophysiology.progression: Can progress to tendinosis if untreated.

name: Bursitis
description: Bursitis is the inflammation of one or more bursae (small sacs) of synovial fluid in the body, commonly caused by repetitive movement or trauma.

epidemiology.prevalence: 1% of adults will experience bursitis at some point
epidemiology.mortality: Bursitis is not typically associated with mortality
epidemiology.age_distribution: Most common in middle-aged and elderly individuals

pathophysiology.mechanism: Inflammation occurs due to repetitive microtrauma or acute injury inciting cytokine production in the synovial lining of the bursa.
pathophysiology.molecular_basis: Involves pro-inflammatory cytokines such as IL-1 and TNF-alpha.
pathophysiology.progression: Can progress from mild inflammation to chronic pain and limited movement if untreated.
